By contrast, incorporated AI-generated content is subject to fixed numerical ceilings (100 words per instance, 10% aggregate), because that narrower, mechanical act of quotation is better suited to a bright-line rule than the broader assistance-versus-substitution question. Mandatory naming, a full prompt-and-response appendix, in-text attribution, and a signed certification convert disclosure into an enforceable condition of the exception itself, so partial compliance affords no defense, and the institution retains audit authority independent of prior suspicion.

The author frames the resulting template as a first iteration, refined through human review and testing against several AI systems (including Harvey AI), to be revised further based on classroom experience.

title: Last in Line: Implicit Racial Bias in Healthcare Scheduling Delays
affiliations: Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU), , Santa Clara University - Information Systems and Analytics and Santa Clara University - Information Systems and Analytics

detail.title: Last in Line: Implicit Racial Bias in Healthcare Scheduling Delays

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants, patients, identifiable personal data, or case studies requiring ethics approval or informed consent.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.
declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: Not applicable. This study is not a clinical trial.

detail.abstract: Problem definition: With recent advances in analytics and data science, it is increasingly common for healthcare appointment scheduling systems to follow a predict-then-optimize framework: historical data are first used to predict patients' individual no-show probabilities, and then an optimization module schedules patients to minimize a weighted total cost of patient waiting time, provider idle time, and provider overtime. This paper identifies and studies a previously unexamined mechanism through which such systems can generate racial disparities. We show that cost-minimizing policies systematically schedule patients at higher risk of no-shows farther into the future while scheduling patients at lower risk of no-shows closer to the present. Because no-show risk is correlated with race and low socioeconomic status, Black patients are consistently assigned longer appointment delays, even when race is not used in the development of these scheduling policies. Methodology/results: We analytically study a single-day scheduling model and establish that increasing the no-show probability of patients at high risk of no-shows while decreasing it for patients at low risk of no-shows weakly decreases schedule cost. Extending the analysis to a multi-day setting, we show that this effect can be achieved by assigning longer appointment delays to patients with higher no-show risk. Using a large real-world data set, our numerical experiments validate that, under a predict-then-optimize framework that excludes race as an input, Black patients are nevertheless assigned delays up to 76% longer compared to non-Black patients. Furthermore, such racial disparities arise consistently across all practice environments tested. Managerial implications: Scheduling systems optimized solely for operational efficiency can generate racial disparities in access to care without any explicit use of race. Our results call for equity-aware scheduling policies and highlight the need for bias audits of (AI-driven) scheduling tools, particularly as regulatory scrutiny of algorithmic discrimination continues to intensify.

title: 3 Musafir: How the Organization Makes Travel for Women in Pakistan
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: 3 Musafir: How the Organization Makes Travel for Women in Pakistan
detail.abstract: Context and Gap: Women’s travel in Pakistan is constrained by safety, permission, and accessibility. While social sustainability, a critical construct, which is often confused with environmental sustainability in touris,m is under-studied, Purpose: This study examined how community-building factors, experience design, safety & permission, community rituals & peer support, and storytelling & branded content operate through trust and community identification to drive repeat participation and advocacy/word-of-mouth in Teen Musafir Research design/Data: We used a cross-sectional survey of 72 participants, analyzed with SEM (AMOS), and triangulated with four brief interviews and field observations. The constructs from the survey were measured on a 5-point Likert scale with acceptable reliability and validity. Results: SEM Results showed that Safety & Permission significantly increased Trust, while Community Rituals & Peer Support strongly increased both Trust and Community Identification. Community Identification was the strongest predictor of both Repeat Participation and Advocacy/Word-of-Mouth. Trust also contributed to Advocacy/Word-of-Mouth, although it did not influence Repeat Participation. Experience Design showed only marginal and non-significant effects on Trust and Community Identification, and Storytelling & Branded Content did not significantly affect either outcome. Safety & Permission also did not contribute substantially to Community Identification. Theory: Findings separate a risk-assurance pathway (Safety/Permission → Trust → Advocacy) from a belonging pathway (Rituals/Support → Community Identification → Repeat & Advocacy) and position community rituals as the primary mechanism for identity formation in women-only experiential travel Practical contribution: Implications include codifying safety-permission protocols, institutionalizing a ritual playbook that reliably fosters belonging, and using storytelling to signal norms and procedures. Value: This is among the first empirical models from Pakistan to explain how community building makes women’s travel socially sustainable via trust and belonging.

title: The Dark Side of Hyper-Personalization: When Campaign Micro-Segmentation Conflicts with Corporate Brand Standardization Strategy

detail.title: The Dark Side of Hyper-Personalization: When Campaign Micro-Segmentation Conflicts with Corporate Brand Standardization Strategy
detail.abstract: The contemporary marketing landscape is increasingly defined by the pursuit of hyperpersonalization, a strategy enabled by big data and artificial intelligence that allows for the micro-segmentation of audiences and the delivery of highly tailored brand messages. While this approach promises unparalleled customer engagement and conversion rates, it introduces a fundamental strategic tension: the conflict between granular, individualized communication and the corporate imperative for a unified, standardized brand identity. This research investigates the "dark side" of hyper-personalization, exploring how aggressive microsegmentation can inadvertently erode a company's core brand equity. Through a conceptual analysis of brand standardization theory and personalization frameworks, this study posits that excessive micro-segmentation can lead to brand fragmentation, where disparate customer experiences dilute the central brand narrative, confuse stakeholder perceptions, and compromise the efficiency of global marketing operations. The research further examines the inherent risks, including algorithmic bias, the creation of 'filter bubbles' that limit brand reach, and the potential for a "brand schizophrenia" effect where the company presents contradictory faces to different consumer groups. By identifying the key points of conflict-ranging from messaging consistency and visual identity to brand values and customer trust-this paper provides a strategic framework for navigating the tension. It concludes that a sustainable brand strategy does not necessitate choosing between personalization and standardization, but rather requires a "smart standardization" approach. This involves defining inviolable brand core elements that remain universal while allowing for flexible, data-informed personalization of peripheral attributes. The findings offer crucial insights for marketing practitioners and scholars, proposing a balanced path that harnesses the power of personalization without sacrificing the foundational integrity and long-term value of a coherent corporate brand.

title: A Study on Competition in the Mobile Ecosystem: Focusing on the Market Dominance of App Stores
affiliations: Korea Development Institute (KDI)

detail.title: A Study on Competition in the Mobile Ecosystem: Focusing on the Market Dominance of App Stores

publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Development Institute (KDI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Using detailed market data, this study provides an in-depth analysis of competition in app store related markets and derives implications for the market dominance of app store platforms. It examines the state of competition both between the app stores of Google and Apple, and among leading apps within them from various perspectives, while also examining where the Korean market diverges from other major markets.

Chapter 2 analyzes the market sizes of Google Play and Apple’s App Store across multiple dimensions, including free versus paid apps, non-game versus game apps, and category-level breakdowns. The relative dominance of each app store varies considerably across countries. In Korea, Google Play accounted for over 70% of both downloads and revenue as of 2023. Across all major countries, the share of free apps has risen steadily in both measures, recently surpassing 98%―a pattern consistent with revenue models anchored in in-app purchases rather than paid app sales. Comparing non-game and game apps, game apps account for 93% of Google Play revenue and 71% of App Store revenue, making them the primary driver of overall revenue growth. Korea stands out in this regard. Not only is the revenue share of game apps disproportionately high relative to major countries, but concentration in a narrow set of top-performing categories is also markedly more pronounced.
Chapter 3 uses app-level performance data for the top 1,000 apps to analyze within-store concentration. The degree of concentration is substantial: these apps account for nearly 100% of revenue and roughly 60% of downloads. When a Pareto distribution is fitted to app performance, the estimated shape parameters fall below 1 in many categories―especially for free downloads―indicating an extreme bias toward top-ranked apps. Revenue distributions are more uneven still for game apps than for non-game apps.

Chapter 4 examines the volatility of app performance rankings, focusing on top-ranked apps. Monthly transition matrices constructed across ranking groups, reveal a tendency for apps to remain within the same ranking group from one month to the next, with persistence more pronounced among higher-ranked groups. Revenue rankings exhibit considerably less volatility than download rankings.

These findings suggest that the app store market is close to a competitive bottleneck, situation in which platforms can exercise strong market dominance over app developers. The heterogeneous user bases of Google Play and the App Store further suggest that inter-store competition for single-homing consumers may be limited. Korea’s market situation heightens these concerns. Compared to other major countries, game apps account for a dominant portion of revenue in Korea, and spending is heavily concentrated in popular categories―particularly games with high in-app purchase volumes. For app stores, this concentration raises the stakes of attracting top game apps; for app developers, it elevates the importance of marketing tools such as chart rankings and featured placements. This environment can amplify both the incentives for and the effects of practices already under scrutiny―mandatory in-app payment requirements, the use of featured placements to exclude rival app stores, and self-preferencing―suggesting a need for close monitoring by competition authorities.

title: Can Customer Ratings be Discrimination Amplifiers? Evidence from a Gig Economy Platform
affiliations: , Yale University and Yale School of Management

detail.title: Can Customer Ratings be Discrimination Amplifiers? Evidence from a Gig Economy Platform
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether rating systems generate discriminatory spillovers and act as "discrimination amplifiers." When platforms display aggregated customer ratings, these "quality metrics" also serve as anchors for future evaluations. Because they embed ratings from biased customers, displayed averages memorialize past discrimination, transmitting it to otherwise unbiased customers and amplifying bias among discriminatory ones. We formalize this mechanism using a stylized analytical model and test it with data from an online labor platform. Allowing for unobserved heterogeneity, we identify three customer segments: a neutral segment, and two biased segments, one that cancels more minority-accepted jobs and another that both cancels more and rates minorities lower. All segments are impacted strongly by displayed ratings. Customer discrimination generates a rating gap of 36.1% and an estimated earnings gap via job loss of 5.2% between minority and majority workers. Notably, the unbiased segment produces discriminatory outcomes through spillovers. Adjusting displayed ratings reduces the gaps by mitigating the spillovers to the unbiased segment and amplification of the biased segments, but aggregate rating and earnings disparities persist because biased segments constitute a large share of the market.

title: Popularizing Sustainable Consumption through Augmented Reality: A Visual and Auditory Sensory Perspective from Indian Online Shoppers
affiliations: REVA University and REVA University

detail.title: Popularizing Sustainable Consumption through Augmented Reality: A Visual and Auditory Sensory Perspective from Indian Online Shoppers
detail.abstract: This study investigates the role of augmented reality (AR) in popularising sustainable consumption through visual and auditory sensory engagement in online shopping, with particular reference to Indian consumers. Moving beyond its conventional commercial applications, AR is conceptualised as a science and technology popularisation tool capable of enhancing public awareness of eco-friendly products and responsible consumption practices. The findings demonstrate that AR-enabled shopping experiencesincorporating immersive 3D visualisations, interactive product trials, and auditory information cuessignificantly influence consumers' purchase decisions toward environmentally sustainable alternatives. By improving product understanding and reducing purchase uncertainty, AR contributes to more informed decision-making and lower product return rates, thereby supporting sustainable resource use. Furthermore, the study highlights the potential of AR to empower rural entrepreneurs, artisans, and small-scale producers by enabling them to present sustainable products to wider audiences in engaging and informative ways. Overall, the research aligns with broader goals of environmental conservation, community development, and sustainable resource management, offering actionable insights for policymakers, educators, and marketers seeking to design socially relevant sustainability initiatives through technology-driven interventions.

title: Technical Specification for the Scientific Discovery Operating System: Mathematical Formalization and Engineering Architecture -A Proceduralized Knowledge Discovery Protocol Based on the Factor Hierarchy Law and Testability Norms

detail.title: Technical Specification for the Scientific Discovery Operating System: Mathematical Formalization and Engineering Architecture -A Proceduralized Knowledge Discovery Protocol Based on the Factor Hierarchy Law and Testability Norms
detail.abstract: Tang (2026g) established the theoretical framework of the Scientific Discovery Operating System, providing the first complete definition of the Factor Hierarchy Law—including the dichotomy of regime factors and execution factors, the three morphologies of regime factors (pure regime factors, dual-identity factors, and pure execution factors), the Testability Principle, the six functional dimensions of the Testability Norms and their core commitment that "functional dimensions are eternal, implementation tools are replaceable," and first establishing testability as the second gateway after Popperian falsifiability, i.e., the third foundation of scientific methodology (following Bacon's experimental method and Popper's falsifiability). Tang (2026r) subsequently positioned the Factor Hierarchy Law as "the law of meta-laws," unified the three components into the Scientific Discovery Operating System, and first proposed the openness of the operating system—that not only the tool layer is replaceable, but the number of functional dimensions themselves may be expanded or streamlined in the future—thereby establishing the fourth foundation of scientific methodology. This paper completes the mathematical formalization and engineering architecture design of the operating system on the basis of the above theoretical foundations, establishing it as a complete technical specification. This paper does not redefine or prove the mathematical kernel of the operating system—the kernel is constituted by the axioms and theorems in Tang (2026g) and Tang (2026r). What this paper defines are the calling interfaces of the kernel, the data flow protocols among modules, and the architectural constraints for engineering implementation. The core contributions include: (1) complete mathematical formalization of the MRSD algorithm (Multi-Regime State Decoupling Algorithm)—the core engine of the operating system responsible for automatically detecting the positions, quantities, and types of regime-switching breakpoints from objective data, including the acceptability conditions for the input data matrix, the mathematical definition of the structural optimization operator with its equivalence declaration to the Bai-Perron algorithm, and the formalized structure of the output regime division matrix; (2) engineering architecture of the audit engine—strict separation of functional requirements (irreplaceable architectural norms) from currently recommended tools (replaceable algorithmic implementations) across four core inspection modules (Search Completeness, Modulation Relation, Structural Breakpoint, Causal Direction), with functional requirements explicitly designated as irreplaceable architectural norms and specific tools designated as currently recommended implementations, and the cross-validation rule of the Structural Breakpoint module precisely defined as multi-category independent tool verification, including behavioral semantics for tie-breaking arbitration and rule weights for activation operator stratification; (3) the Tool-Layer Replaceability Principle—tools may be replaced under the condition of satisfying functional requirement constraints, with equivalence verification on standard datasets required before replacement, and tool divergence itself identifying regions requiring further investigation; (4) formalized declaration of the operating system as an open protocol—output reliability depends solely on the objectivity of the input data and the transparency of the algorithmic structure; (5) complete mapping between engineering modules and cross-disciplinary verification—demonstrating the precise correspondence between each engineering module and the twenty-five empirical papers; (6) comprehensive tool-layer summary—systematically organizing all tools actually used across the twenty-five papers, classified by the six functional dimensions; (7) prospective outlook—based on the verified theoretical foundations, envisioning the potential impacts of full deployment of the operating system and clarifying the verification pathway from blueprint to reality. Upon completion of these tasks, any competent software engineer may independently implement an operating system normatively equivalent to that described in this paper, relying only on this paper, Tang (2026g), and Tang (2026r). The reliability of this system is jointly guaranteed by rigorous mathematical structure, statistical foundations, and cross-disciplinary empirical verification.

title: An Overview of Robinhood Earn
affiliations: University of Florida and

detail.title: An Overview of Robinhood Earn
detail.abstract: Robinhood Earn is a feature of the Robinhood application, launched on July 1, 2026, through which eligible United States customers earn yield on the Global Dollar stablecoin (USDG). This paper explains what composes Robinhood Earn, how the relevant parts of the Morpho lending protocol work, how the advertised 7% rate is produced, and what onchain data from the program's first month show.

title: How Mechanistic Explanations Reshape Learning and Behavior: Evidence from a Fertilizer Choice Experiment in Eastern Uganda
affiliations: Stanford University, Princeton University - Princeton University, Stanford University, Harvard University - Harvard Graduate School of Education, Oregon State University, Agriworks Uganda and Makerere University, Kampala

detail.title: How Mechanistic Explanations Reshape Learning and Behavior: Evidence from a Fertilizer Choice Experiment in Eastern Uganda
detail.abstract: Mechanistic explanations-descriptions of a system through the causal interactions of its parts-play a key role in human cognition and scientific progress. Despite their importance, we lack systematic evidence on whether and how mechanistic explanations help lay decision-makers interpret information in complex economic environments. We evaluate the causal impact of including mechanistic explanations in an information intervention: public demonstrations of fertilizer use for smallholder tomato farmers in Eastern Uganda. In all demonstrations, extension officers showcased the impact of a recommended fertilizer recipe. In the treatment group, officers also explained the mechanisms underlying the recipe's effects-introducing the language of macronutrients and the causal processes linking nutrients, soil features, and plant growth. We collected detailed data on beliefs and behaviors from 797 farmers in a lab-in-the-field experiment conducted at the demonstration site and followed up with them over two growing seasons. In the lab-in-the-field, treated farmers generalized more effectively-making better substitution and arbitrage decisions among fertilizers and achieving 9% higher simulated profits in an incentivized fertilizer-application task. At endline, treated farmers' real fertilizer choices reflected improved nutrient timing and balance, and their yields were 14% higher. * Job Market Paper. We are grateful to Agriworks Uganda for an incredible partnership-organizing the demonstrations, mobilizing farmers and providing for their comfort, connecting us with agronomists and extension officers, and more. We would particularly like to acknowledge the outstanding efforts of Boaz Otieno and Emma Wataka. We also thank the survey firms Matrice360 and VIE for maintaining high standards while nimbly navigating field challenges. We especially recognize our field and data managers, Henry Mulissa and Patrick Minja, for their close attention to data quality and strong on-theground judgment. We are very grateful to Sara Restrepo-Tamayo for her generous guidance on materials and logistics, and for coordinating the many moving parts of a challenging pilot. We thank ProsperPlay for developing a user-friendly digital fertilizer-application tool. Sankar thanks his advising committee for their invaluable guidance.

title: Excess Movement in High-frequency Prediction-market Quotes: The Entry-delay Frontier
affiliations: Lehigh University

detail.title: Excess Movement in High-frequency Prediction-market Quotes: The Entry-delay Frontier
detail.abstract: High-frequency prediction-market studies often treat displayed quotes as prices one could trade at. We show that this can produce both excess movement and what looks like profit from mean reversion. In 7,118 Polymarket sports contracts, the aggregate ratio of realized variance to the binary variance budget is 1.53 at one-minute sampling, but 1.05 at sixty minutes. We regroup the known finite-grid identity into two parts, initial calibration and the cross-products of returns, and then split the second part by lag. Miscalibration is small. The excess sits at short lags, and it rejects a joint null: quote error with zero mean and no dependence over time, a martingale fair value, and error orthogonal to that fair value. Under that null the return cross-moment must vanish beyond lag one, whatever the error variance does. We measure it as non-zero at lag two. Serially correlated error remains viable. We then price a ten-point one-minute midpoint fade against 1,153,546 transaction records. Across 36 entry-delay and holding-horizon policies, applied to 3,000 signals in 396 markets, every estimated policy P&L is negative. The best is-0.327 points [-0.70, +0.04], and simultaneous inference does not exclude zero. Among tape-covered signals, 39% carry no transaction at all, and their midpoint reversion is 5.234 points against 1.069 when an entry print exists. High-frequency excess movement on thin books can therefore reflect quote dynamics alone. Those dynamics need not stand for transactions, nor for returns one could have earned at observed transaction prices.

title: Strengthened Regulation and the Survival Dilemma of the Private Economy: Law Enforcement Paradoxes and Governance Reflections During Economic Downturns --An Analysis Based on the Three-Level Prisoner's Decision Trap Theory
affiliations: Zhongnan University of Economics and Law

detail.title: Strengthened Regulation and the Survival Dilemma of the Private Economy: Law Enforcement Paradoxes and Governance Reflections During Economic Downturns --An Analysis Based on the Three-Level Prisoner's Decision Trap Theory

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.
declarations.funderStatement: This study does not involve human participants, and no additional ethics approval is required.

detail.abstract: Amid mounting cyclical downward pressures on China’s economy, the regulatory and law enforcement system has witnessed unprecedented intensification. From intensive penalties against listed firms and retroactive tax recovery targeting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), to criminal prosecutions of corporate controllers and rent-seeking law enforcement against individual industrial and commercial households, strengthened regulation coincides with economic recession, forming a profound governance paradox. This raises a fundamental question: why do some governance systems intensify regulation rather than reduce burdens on enterprises during periods of economic stress?Drawing on the theoretical framework of the ThreeLevel Prisoner’s Decision Trap (PDP) proposed by Dianping Xu, this paper systematically analyzes the evolutionary trajectory of regulatory enforcement intensity in China since the COVID-19 outbreak in 2020 and its mechanisms impacting the private economy. The study finds that post-pandemic regulatory enforcement has undergone three phases: emergency leniency, comprehensive tightening, and standardized rectification. Driven by fiscal strains, some local governments and law enforcement agencies have fallen into a myopic trap of “generating revenue through penalties”. At the micro level, survival pressures and assessment incentives for frontline law enforcement officers breed rent-seeking law enforcement. At the meso level, reliance on fines and confiscation revenues solidifies organizational path dependence. At the macro level, non-cooperative games among multiple stakeholders trigger the overall deterioration of the business environment. Using empirical evidence including surging administrative penalties on listed companies in 2025, cases of retroactive tax recovery, and criminal prosecutions for internal corruption in private enterprises, this paper reveals how strengthened regulation, through successive evolution of the decision trap, ultimately undermines private entrepreneurs’ confidence and long-term economic growth potential. This research offers a new theoretical lens for understanding the “regulation-growth” paradox in China’s economic governance, and puts forward policy proposals to optimize enterprise-related law enforcement and balance regulatory effectiveness with economic development.

title: Distributional Regime Persistence: Geometric Market Memory and Its Forecasting Limits

detail.title: Distributional Regime Persistence: Geometric Market Memory and Its Forecasting Limits
detail.abstract:
We define distributional regime persistence as the duration for which a rolling empirical return distribution remains geometrically aligned with a high-volatility prototype. Building on Wasserstein market-regime clustering, we estimate low- and high-volatility barycenters from rolling return distributions and locate each window between them using a normalized relative-distance score. This score yields distributional recovery times and cumulative excess memory that can be compared with filtered high-state probabilities from an ordered, variance-targeted Markov-switching GJR-GARCH model.

Daily returns for the S&P 500, FTSE 100, Nikkei 225, and Hang Seng from January 2000 through June 2026 produce three main findings. First, raw distributional persistence is strongly scale-related: log realized volatility explains 59.5%–74.3% of its in-sample variation, while a conditional shape-only score retains modest residual information. Second, FTSE and Nikkei produce negative recovery gaps across alternative thresholds and geometries, but their bootstrap intervals include zero; the negative direction appears in 82%–85% of replications. S&P 500 COVID provides the strongest inferential result: its distribution-lagging gap has a 95% bootstrap interval of 4–94 trading days and is positive in 98.5% of replications. Hang Seng Markov-switching estimates are weakly identified and excluded from parametric inference. Third, observed DRP persistence exceeds an overlapping-window IID Student-t null. In a real-time forecast design with pre-2007 fixed prototypes, a multi-horizon volatility benchmark, expanding and rolling estimation, and MSE, MAE, and QLIKE losses, however, DRP produces no stable incremental forecast gain.

The evidence supports DRP as a measurement and model-diagnostic framework—not as a new clustering claim or a universal forecasting improvement. The negative forecast result is an informational boundary: geometric alignment describes the realized state and model disagreement, but it is not an omitted volatility factor once multi-horizon volatility history is observed.

title: Theoretical Extensions and Methodological Output of the Quantum-Classical Hybrid: The Regime-Factor Purity Spectrum, the Binary Structure of the Confirmed-Breakpoint Network, and Cross-Disciplinary Predictions --Paradigm Deepening, Testable Predictions, and Complete Deployment of the Operating System Based on the Triple Demotion

detail.title: Theoretical Extensions and Methodological Output of the Quantum-Classical Hybrid: The Regime-Factor Purity Spectrum, the Binary Structure of the Confirmed-Breakpoint Network, and Cross-Disciplinary Predictions --Paradigm Deepening, Testable Predictions, and Complete Deployment of the Operating System Based on the Triple Demotion
detail.abstract: Tang (2026x) completed the triple demotion of the nuclear shell—the shell model was proven to be the projection of the regime-switch network in the spherical-symmetry limit by the 3.68–9.68-fold amplification of the Chow F of the five traditional magic numbers under continuous sphericity weighting (independently reproducible), the liquid drop model was proven to be the projection of the regime-switch network in the classical limit, and the independent-particle-motion axiom was proven to be incomplete. On this theoretical foundation, this paper accomplishes three independent theoretical extensions. First—the cross-disciplinary corollary of the regime-factor purity spectrum. The confirmed-breakpoint spacing CV = 0.67 falls between the purely discrete (particle-physics color-charge three-state CV = 0; chemical valence-electron equal-spacing CV = 0) and the purely continuous synthetic baseline (CV median = 0.689). Based on the regime-factor purities of six disciplines, the purity spectrum is formally proposed—from the fully continuous regime factors of finance to the purely discrete regime factors of particle physics and chemistry—providing a unified explanatory framework for the differentiation of demotion types: purely discrete regime factors permit constructive derivational demotion, semi-continuous regime factors permit limit-degradation derivational demotion, and fully continuous regime factors permit paradigm demotion. This purity spectrum supplies a testable predictive framework for the deployment of the Factor Hierarchy Law in a seventh discipline. The binary structure of the confirmed-breakpoint network—five confirmed breakpoints forming the full-N-axis skeleton (spacing CV = 0.67) and fifteen candidate breakpoints filling the inter-skeleton gaps (mean spacing 9.7)—is identified as a distinctive organizational feature of semi-continuous regime factors, standing in sharp contrast to the equal-spacing regime grids of purely discrete regime factors. Second—methodological insights into the paradigm shift. The stark contrast between the WLS continuous-weight approach and the doubly-magic-enrichment binary-screening approach (amplification of 3.68–9.68-fold versus 0.01–0.05-fold) reveals the deep physical implication that "the spherical-symmetry limit is a weight, not a region"—sphericity is continuous, and the applicability of the shell model is continuous. The cross-disciplinary methodological value of activation-operator stratification is systematically articulated for the first time: inv-family operators are sensitive to the quantum region, and raw-family operators are sensitive to the classical region—this stratification provides a direct operational guide for selecting optimal statistical detectors in other disciplines. The uniqueness of the double-track intersection point N≈70.8 is demonstrated by an elimination-method proof using the seven-metric intersection matrix—the intersection point between the shell-correction energy ΔR² and the intercept/slope ratio is the only metric pair among twenty-one pairs with a clear and stable intersection characteristic; this elimination method can be generalized to other disciplines to locate quantum-classical equilibrium points. Third—the concretization of cross-disciplinary predictions and the complete deployment of the operating system. The mid-shell silence zone is proposed as a testable cross-disciplinary hypothesis for quantum-classical hybrid systems—the silence zone within nuclear physics has been confirmed by multi-operator cross-validation, and numerical simulations of a dual-signal mixing model confirm the statistical principle that "mixed signals systematically suppress the Chow F," but its applicability in condensed matter physics and quantum chemistry depends on confirmation by independent experiments. The QCTI index provides a cross-disciplinarily universal quantitative framework for the degree of quantum-classical mixing—the simplified QCTI (requiring only macroscopic-model residuals plus discrete markers, ρ = −0.93) can be directly deployed in any system with an analogous structure, and its applicability boundary is precisely defined as "requiring a macroscopic baseline with R² > 0.9." The complete deployment of the Factor Hierarchy Law operating system in nuclear physics—all six functional dimensions fully covered by over twenty distinct tools—and the unique methodological contributions of the nuclear-physics deployment provide a complete operational guide for the deployment of the Factor Hierarchy Law in a seventh discipline.

title: Causal Effects of Financial Assistance and Small and Medium Enterprise Turnover During Crises
affiliations: , Macquarie University, Macquarie Business School, Macquarie University, Macquarie Business School and Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University (XJTLU)

detail.title: Causal Effects of Financial Assistance and Small and Medium Enterprise Turnover During Crises

declarations.funderStatement: This research uses data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) Business Longitudinal Analysis Data Environment (BLADE). The authors acknowledge the ABS for access to confidentialised microdata and the support provided through the ABS DataLab. This research was supported by the Australian Research Council (ARC) under a Discovery Project (DP230101282). The results and views expressed are those of the authors and do not represent the views of either ABS or the funding body.

detail.abstract: We analyse the causal impact of emergency government policy on small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) performance during systemic crises, using Australia's COVID-19 fiscal response as a natural experiment. Drawing on firm-level panel data for 1,859 SMEs from the Australian Business Longitudinal Analysis Data Environment (2018-2021), we implement a Doubly Robust Difference-in-Differences design to estimate the short- and medium-term effects of crisis-related financial assistance on firm turnover. We find, first, that the aggregate package of COVID-19 support measures did not, on average, increase SME turnover relative to non-recipient firms. Second, policy effects differ by instrument: tax concessions generated a statistically significant but temporary increase in turnover, whereas direct subsidies had no measurable impact. Third, the positive effects of tax concessions dissipated within one year of receipt. Fourth, treatment effects are heterogeneous, with smaller and younger firms exhibiting stronger turnover responses than larger and more established firms. While certain tax-based measures can provide short-run revenue stabilisation, broad-based financial assistance does not necessarily translate into sustained improvements in SME performance during economic crises.

title: Relation between Nutritional Factors & Stunting in Adolescents: A cross-sectional study among school-going students of 10-16 years old in a selected school of Dhaka city, Bangladesh
affiliations: Leeds Trinity University, University of Dhaka, University of Dhaka and University of Dhaka

detail.title: Relation between Nutritional Factors & Stunting in Adolescents: A cross-sectional study among school-going students of 10-16 years old in a selected school of Dhaka city, Bangladesh
detail.abstract: Background:Adolescent stunting remains a persistent public health concern in Bangladesh, reflecting chronic nutritional deprivation and inadequate dietary quality. Although extensive research has addressed early childhood malnutrition, evidence on nutritional determinants of adolescent stunting remains limited.Objective:This study aimed to analyse the relationship between nutritional factors and stunting among adolescents aged (10-16) years) in Bangladesh.Methods:A cross-sectional analytical design was employed among school-going adolescents aged 10-16 years. Anthropometric measurements were converted to height-for-age Z-scores using WHO standards. Data on dietary intake, food diversity, and meal frequency were collected through structured questionnaires. Logistic regression was used to identify nutritional factors significantly associated with stunting.Results:Preliminary findings indicate that approximately one-third of adolescents were stunted, It also revealed that weekly high frequency dietary intake of specific foods (P<0.05), dietary diversity score (P<0.05), physical activity level (P<0.05) and hygiene practices (P=0.05) were negatively related to adolescent stunting.Conclusions:Nutritional factors like Dietary Diversity Scores (DDS), frequency of specific diet found to be important factors among adolescents stunting rather than socioeconomic factors alone. Improving dietary diversity, promoting balanced school meals, and integrating adolescent nutrition into national health programs are essential strategies to reduce growth faltering and break the intergenerational cycle of undernutrition.

title: Are You Okay? Effects of a National Peer-Support Campaign on Mental Health
affiliations: Monash University - Centre for Health Economics, , Monash University - Centre for Health Economics and Monash University - Centre for Health Economics, University of Zurich - Department of Economics

detail.title: Are You Okay? Effects of a National Peer-Support Campaign on Mental Health
detail.abstract: National public health awareness campaigns that emphasize peer-to-peer support are increasingly adopted, but evidence on the effects of peer-based programs at scale remains limited. Using quasi-experimental methods, we examine whether the prominent nationwide “R U OK? Day” campaign affects short-term mental health outcomes in Australia. Leveraging survey and administrative data, we find R U OK? Day leads to a 4% of a standard deviation increase in self-reported mental wellbeing, with the effect particularly pronounced among middle-aged males who experience a 9\% of a standard deviation increase. We find no detectable effects on mental health care utilization, and we detect no statistically significant changes in suicide-related deaths in the short run, though the mortality outcomes are rare and power is limited. Our results underscore that peer-based campaigns can improve mental wellbeing, especially for high-risk groups, and point to a distinction between short-run psychological responses and outcomes that require behavioural follow-through.

title: A Simulation Game for Water Security and Resilience Education
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: A Simulation Game for Water Security and Resilience Education
detail.abstract: This study presents the development and implementation of a novel simulation-based game designed to enhance engineering students' competencies in systems thinking, environmental impact assessment, critical thinking, and social responsibility, aligned with the Engineering for One Planet (EOP) learning outcomes framework. The game addresses water security and resilience within a river basin, emphasizing the design of effective water conservation incentives under conditions of uncertain and recurring drought. Gameplay incorporates multiple stakeholder perspectives, including farmers, non-governmental organizations, and state-level governmental entities, each characterized by distinct objectives, resource constraints, and behavioral attributes. The simulation integrates global and local system variables and evaluates performance metrics such as optimality gap and water conservation rate. Players receive real-time feedback through interactive dashboards and are exposed to optimal policy solutions derived from game-theoretic models, enabling engagement with complex socio-environmental tradeoffs and informed decision-making under uncertainty. The game is available in English, Portuguese, and Spanish, supporting broader accessibility and deployment across diverse classroom settings. To evaluate game effectiveness, a summative evaluation was conducted using pre-and post-course surveys administered to 69 master's students enrolled in the Data Analytics program. Statistical analysis indicates significant improvements in students' abilities to understand complex interdependencies within agricultural water systems, assess environmental impacts, apply critical reasoning, and recognize social dimensions of sustainability. Text mining of open-ended survey responses further revealed that 73% of students expressed a strong interest at the intersection of artificial intelligence, resilience, and sustainability.

title: Balancing Safety and Innovation? The Interaction between the Regulatory and Liability Frameworks for AI Medical Devices
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Balancing Safety and Innovation? The Interaction between the Regulatory and Liability Frameworks for AI Medical Devices
detail.abstract: This paper examines the interaction between the revised EU Product Liability Directive, and the Medical Device Regulation and AI Act. It focuses on how this legal regime shapes the balance between patient safety and innovation for AI-driven Medical Devices. The analysis utilises liability mechanisms to assess how liability exposure can reinforce regulatory duties, while also considering safeguards intended to preserve innovation. However, it does not claim that safety and innovation are mutually exclusive. Rather, it emphasises the strong incentives towards risk minimisation as a result of liability exposure. This could potentially lead to a preference for incremental development in the field and more limited access to disruptive medical technologies in the EU.

title: Flexibility Spillovers: Work from Home and Moonlighting

detail.title: Flexibility Spillovers: Work from Home and Moonlighting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number 24KJ0641 and JST SPRING Grant Number JPMJSP2108.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether employer-granted work-from-home (WfH) access changes paid work outside the primary job. Using a 2016-2019 pre-pandemic panel of Japanese workers, I exploit staggered transitions into WfH permission in a dynamic difference-indifferences design. WfH permission increases moonlighting participation, weekly side-job hours, and real side-job earnings, with no statistically significant decline in primary-job hours or earnings accompanying the increase in moonlighting. The participation response is concentrated in employee side jobs involving tasks similar to those in the primary job, while motive-specific estimates show an increase in financially motivated side jobs. Together, these findings show that flexibility in the primary job can expand paid work outside the primary employer, with the response centered on earning additional income from familiar tasks rather than on career experimentation or self-employment.

title: Property Rights and Innovation Dynamism: The Role of Women Inventors
affiliations: Cardiff University - Cardiff Business School

detail.title: Property Rights and Innovation Dynamism: The Role of Women Inventors
detail.abstract: To what extent do inclusive institutions explain innovations? This paper examines the Married Women's Property Acts, which granted US women independent property rights during the nineteenth century. Using the universe of patents and a staggered-adoption design, I show that the reforms led to a substantial increase in women's patenting, with effects peaking about a decade after enactment. A backof-the-envelope calculation suggests that these laws account for at least one-third of women's nineteenth-century innovations. Women's inventions contributed to the volume of innovations without displacing men and their innovations were equally novel. I further implement triple-difference analysis with men and a neighborcounty border design; both confirming the women-specific reform effects. Mechanism analyses indicate that the Acts strengthened incentives and relaxed marital constraints: the likelihood of observing married women inventors-including those with children-rises after the reform. An establishment-level TFP analysis suggests positive association between property rights and productivity levels among womenowned establishments within related industries, speaking to the welfare effects of property rights.

title: The Arbitrary Myth: Challenging Trademark Law's Elevation of Arbitrary Marks
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - University of North Carolina School of Law

detail.title: The Arbitrary Myth: Challenging Trademark Law's Elevation of Arbitrary Marks
detail.abstract:
Under its Abercrombie spectrum, trademark law grants "arbitrary" marks-like APPLE for computers or AMAZON for retail-its highest form of protection, treating them as equivalent to fanciful marks such as KODAK or EXXON. This Article challenges that foundational assumption. Unlike fanciful marks, which are invented and enjoy strong source-identifying capacity due to their novelty, arbitrary marks draw on existing language through catachresis: a rhetorical move that repurposes a common word in novel commercial context. In doing so, arbitrary marks generate layered metaphoric meanings that more closely resemble the associative leaps of suggestive marks, rather than the invented distinctiveness of fanciful ones.

Empirical research supports this reframing. Studies show that arbitrary marks underperform in measures of consumer recognition and brand clarity, casting doubt on their presumed strength. Yet despite these shortcomings, they remain doctrinally privileged—largely, this Article argues, because the trademark system needs them. With trademark depletion and congestion accelerating, arbitrary marks offer a convenient legal loophole, allowing brand owners to appropriate familiar language without the evidentiary burden of proving secondary meaning. As a result, brand owners are incentivized to choose arbitrary marks for their high protectability grades, often to their own market detriment.

This dynamic also carries broader cultural costs. When ordinary words like AMAZON or APPLE become proprietary, they displace shared meanings, subordinating public language to private branding. Trademark law, in this way, channels cultural symbols into commercial use to keep pace with semiotic demand. This Article argues for a doctrinal recalibration: arbitrary marks should be treated as presumptively weaker than fanciful ones—at or around the level of suggestive marks. More broadly, this inquiry exposes the conceptual fragility of the Abercrombie spectrum itself, and calls for a more honest reckoning with the values trademark law protects—and those it displaces.

title: A Gamification Approach to Resource Allocation for Resilient Interdependent Infrastructures
affiliations: , , George Mason University and

detail.title: A Gamification Approach to Resource Allocation for Resilient Interdependent Infrastructures
detail.abstract: Gamification offers a dynamic framework for analyzing decision-making processes in critical infrastructure systems. Restoration and maintenance decisions of these systems are typically managed at the municipal level and are often decentralized. While there is extensive research on optimizing restoration strategies to enhance infrastructure performance, many studies rely on centralized mathematical models that overlook dynamic interactions and human factors essential to comprehend the evolution of decisions. To help bridge this gap, we develop a simulation-based game providing players (e.g., municipal administrators) with a feedback-rich environment for testing their restoration strategies. The proposed game incorporates Systems Engineering Verification and Validation (V&V) practices and was informed by our collaboration with Arlington County's Department of Public Safety Communications and Emergency Management in Virginia. It is powered by an agent-based simulation that models interdependent water distribution and road networks, capturing both the behavior of infrastructure components and players' interactions with them. We evaluated the performance of the game with both experts from Arlington County and students from the Operations Research/ Computer Science programs. We then compared their strategies with optimal restoration sequences derived from the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) model to understand how players approach the restoration decisions differently. Statistical analyses were conducted using the post and pre-game survey to evaluate learning outcomes and to compare decision making behaviors between experts and the students.

title: Charter Drift in Frontier AI Governance A Falsifiable Framework for Institutional Integrity under Commercial Pressure

detail.title: Charter Drift in Frontier AI Governance A Falsifiable Framework for Institutional Integrity under Commercial Pressure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is Founder and CEO of Argus Intelligence Group, an independent research and advisory entity, and Chief Technology Officer of Gemini Industries Inc. Neither entity has commercial or contracting relationships with the frontier AI developers named in this paper (Alibaba, Amazon, Anthropic, DeepSeek, Google, IBM, Meta, Microsoft, Mistral, OpenAI, Stability AI, Writer, xAI) that would create a financial interest in the paper's conclusions. The author has no personal or financial relationship with the individuals or institutions named in the paper's analysis of the FASCSA-Anthropic proceedings. The framework presented is offered as independent scholarly work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was self-funded and conducted independently through Argus Intelligence Group. No external funding, grant support, or institutional sponsorship contributed to the preparation of this paper.

detail.abstract: Frontier AI governance institutions face a structural problem that classical regulatory theory names but current policy discourse has not internalized: the drift of governance bodies from their founding charter toward the preservation of their method, their institutional survival, or the interests of the entities they were established to govern. Drawing on Stigler's regulatory capture theory (1971), Jensen and Meckling's agency framework (1976), and DiMaggio and Powell's institutional isomorphism (1983), this paper proposes a falsifiable framework-the Charter Drift Framework-for identifying when a frontier AI governance institution has failed its mission while preserving its method. The framework identifies three failure modes: Method Lock-In, Refusal of Cost, and Absent Method. It specifies five empirical conditions any credible governance body must demonstrate: Binding External Veto, Costly Truth-Disclosure, Method Sacrifice Under Stress, Ceded Inspectability, and Protected Dissent Throughput. It applies a three-gate anti-gaming filter (costly, irreversible, externally verifiable) to distinguish substantive from performative compliance. The Foundation Model Transparency Index decline from a mean of 58/100 in 2024 to 40.69/100 in 2025, alongside IBM's counterexample score of 95/100, provides empirical grounding. 1 The framework is self-applying: it specifies its own conditions of falsification. The paper concludes with implications for federal acquisition policy, the Foundation Model Transparency Act, and the emerging institutional landscape around sovereign AI capability. It is offered as a companion to the author's Sovereign AI Capability Imperative (SSRN, May 2026).

title: Infrastructure as a Long-Term Asset Class: A Case for Brownfield Infrastructure Reallocation by Sovereign Wealth Funds in a High-Rate Regime

detail.title: Infrastructure as a Long-Term Asset Class: A Case for Brownfield Infrastructure Reallocation by Sovereign Wealth Funds in a High-Rate Regime
detail.abstract: The post-pandemic shift from a near-zero-rate environment to one of persistent inflation and elevated risk-free rates has caused the breakdown of the traditional equity-bond diversification that sovereign wealth fund portfolios have traditionally relied upon. This paper argues that sovereign wealth funds should selectively reallocate towards brownfield infrastructure, operational assets with demand-inelastic, inflation-linked cash flows, as a response to this structural shift. Using stylised frameworks, the paper compares brownfield and greenfield infrastructure under varying monetary tightening scenarios. The analysis has found that greenfield assets require a cash-flow premium to ensure parity with baseline brownfield asset rates, which compounds when the construction delays lengthen. Under the model, brownfield infrastructure NPV remains resilient across all tested scenarios while disproportionately affecting greenfield infrastructure NPV. While illustrative rather than calibrated, the data support a case for brownfield infrastructure against the current macroeconomic context.

title: Taxation and Reallocation in the Secondary Market for Capital Goods
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: Taxation and Reallocation in the Secondary Market for Capital Goods
detail.abstract: This paper studies how the tax system shapes capital reallocation. In a general equilibrium model featuring a realistic tax system, I show that investment subsidies and corporate tax cuts increase capital formation but may decrease reallocation and entry. By contrast, subsidies for used asset purchases unambiguously increase reallocation. I use asset-level data from financed equipment transactions in Texas, firm-level data from Compustat, and industry-level data from the Business Dynamics Statistics to test the theory. I find that assets exposed to larger investment subsidies transact less, firms more exposed to investment subsidies invest more but have lower capital sales, and more-exposed industries experience persistently lower entry. Consistent with theory, these patterns reverse after the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, which reduced the corporate tax rate and extended full expensing to used asset purchases.

title: Demography in a K-Shaped Nation: How Population Change Will Reshape American Economic, Political, and Social Systems, 2026-2050

detail.title: Demography in a K-Shaped Nation: How Population Change Will Reshape American Economic, Political, and Social Systems, 2026-2050
detail.abstract:
America's demographic challenge is not simply that the population is aging or that population growth is slowing. It is that the nation's principal economic, political, and social institutions were built during eight decades of sustained demographic expansion and continue to operate under assumptions of growing workforces, expanding tax bases, rising student enrollments, and robust family support networks. This paper argues that the central issue through 2050 is therefore one of institutional adaptation rather than demographic change alone.

The paper develops an integrated analytical framework that examines how demographic deceleration propagates through federal entitlement programs, labor markets, education, political representation, state and local government finance, housing, healthcare, and household caregiving. It introduces the concept of a K-shaped nation to explain why similar demographic pressures produce increasingly unequal outcomes across regions and communities. Communities with strong fiscal resources, diversified economies, and resilient institutions are generally better positioned to adapt, while those with weaker institutional capacity face self-reinforcing cycles of population loss, labor shortages, service contraction, and fiscal stress.

A central finding is that the burden of demographic adjustment progressively shifts downward through American society. Federal fiscal pressures become state budget challenges. State constraints become municipal service reductions. Municipal limitations increasingly become household responsibilities. At each stage, the institution receiving the burden typically possesses fewer financial, institutional, and human resources than the institution passing it along.

The paper distinguishes between financial constraints and real resource constraints. While fiscal policy can redistribute claims on future output, it cannot by itself create caregivers, healthcare capacity, housing, or functioning local institutions. Immigration can expand the working-age population within a relatively short period, whereas fertility policies require decades to affect labor supply. Artificial intelligence may increase productivity in many sectors but is unlikely to eliminate shortages in occupations requiring sustained physical presence, including caregiving, nursing, construction, and other essential services.

The paper concludes that America's demographic future is unusually predictable because the cohorts that will shape the next two decades have largely already been born. The principal policy challenge is therefore not forecasting demographic change, but adapting institutions built for an era of continuous growth to one of demographic deceleration and, in many places, demographic contraction. Whether demographic change becomes a manageable transition or an increasingly unequal redistribution of economic and social burdens will depend largely on the nation's capacity for institutional adaptation.

Use of AI Tools: Large language model tools were used during the preparation of this manuscript as research and editorial assistants. They assisted with organizing material, identifying potential sources and lines of inquiry, critiquing drafts, checking internal consistency, improving exposition, and suggesting alternative wording.

The paper’s conceptual framework, analytical judgments, interpretation of evidence, policy conclusions, and final editorial decisions are solely those of the author. AI-generated material was reviewed, revised, and, where appropriate, rejected or rewritten by the author before inclusion. The author reviewed cited sources against original publications or authoritative repositories wherever reasonably possible and assumes full responsibility for the accuracy of the analysis, citations, interpretations, and any remaining errors.

Generative AI tools did not exercise independent scholarly judgment and are not authors of this work.

reference: Virginia Public Law and Legal Theory Research Paper Forthcoming
title: The Dragon Who Wasn't
affiliations: Weil, Gotshal & Manges LLP, Government of the State of Delaware - Court of Chancery and University of Virginia School of Law

detail.title: The Dragon Who Wasn't

publicationDetails.detailsText: Virginia Public Law and Legal Theory Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Virginia Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Section 205 of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts declares that every contract imposes a duty on the parties to act in good faith toward and deal fairly with their counterparties. Over the past forty-five years, courts in most states have accepted that declaration as black-letter law, yet have never clearly articulated what the duty actually means. The Restatement drafters envisioned something ambitious: an affirmative covenant that would permit courts to police opportunism by imposing and enforcing community standards of decency, fairness, and reasonableness. Today, that view of the implied covenant is a myth. It persists as legend, but not in the doctrine's application in major U.S. jurisdictions. Dragged from its cave, the fire-breathing, implied-covenant dragon turns out to be a tamed and useful animal. Courts deploy it for the pedestrian purpose of implying terms necessary to give effect to the contract's express provisions, and sometimes to constrain extreme examples of opportunism. Drawing on the doctrine's history, the law of several jurisdictions, and interviews with deal lawyers, this article reveals the dragon for what it is, despite what it may be called.

title: PiDDM: Physics-Informed Differentiable Degradation Modeling for Lithium-Ion Battery State-of-Health Prediction
affiliations: University of Notre Dame, University of Texas at Dallas, The University of Texas at Dallas, University of Texas at Dallas, University of Notre Dame and University of Notre Dame

detail.title: PiDDM: Physics-Informed Differentiable Degradation Modeling for Lithium-Ion Battery State-of-Health Prediction
detail.abstract: Accurate prediction of lithium-ion battery state-of-health (SOH) is essential for the reliable operation of modern energy storage systems. However, purely data-driven machine learning models often generalize poorly across different cycling protocols and may produce physically implausible predictions during long-term extrapolation. To address these limitations, we developed a physics-informed differentiable degradation modeling framework (PiDDM) for lithium-ion battery SOH degradation prediction. The proposed framework incorporates empirical Arrhenius degradation kinetics associated with solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) growth and loss of lithium inventory (LLI) into the neural network training objective. By embedding this degradation regularization into the loss function, PiDDM encourages physically consistent monotonic capacity fade under diverse operating conditions. We evaluate the model on a public dataset containing 55 batteries cycled under six distinct operating protocols. PiDDM achieves the lowest average prediction error compared to other existing models, outperforming both a standard multilayer perceptron (MLP) and a baseline physics-informed neural network (PINN), with a substantially reduced mean squared error. In extrapolation tests, the models are trained on only the first 90\% of each battery’s cycle life and evaluated on the remaining unseen 10\%. Under this setting, PiDDM accurately captures the accelerated end-of-life degradation while avoiding the non-physical capacity regeneration observed in the baseline models. These results demonstrate that incorporating degradation physics into neural network training improves both predictive accuracy and physical consistency, providing a promising framework for practical battery health monitoring.

title: The Impact of BRAC's Online Skills Training Initiative on Youth Income and Employment during COVID-19: A Difference-in-Differences Analysis

detail.title: The Impact of BRAC's Online Skills Training Initiative on Youth Income and Employment during COVID-19: A Difference-in-Differences Analysis
detail.abstract: When COVID-19 closed Bangladesh's training institutions in March 2020, the BRAC Skills Development Program created a skills training initiative called "BISD Online". This paper estimates the impact of that online skills training on the monthly income and employment of disadvantaged youth using a difference-indifferences (DiD) design. The "treatment" group comprises 110 learners who completed the three-month training (January-March 2021); the "comparison" group comprises 58 youths who registered for the same training through an identical process but could not enrol owing to seat unavailability. Incomes are observed in December 2020 (pre-programme) and April 2021 (postprogramme). Estimating the canonical two-group, two-period DiD by ordinary least squares with standard errors clustered at the individual level, the study finds that the training raised participants' monthly income by BDT 1,052 (95% CI: 310-1,795), roughly 116% of the baseline mean, and raised the probability of having any earnings by 12.7 percentage points, nearly a tripling of the employment rate. The estimates are robust to covariate adjustment, an inverse-hyperbolic-sine transformation of income, first-difference and ANCOVA specifications, and Fisher-style randomization inference (p = 0.017). Effects are concentrated among learners who were unemployed at baseline. Because the postprogramme survey fell within a strict nationwide lockdown, during which the "comparison" group's income declined, the DiD estimator nets out this common shock.

title: The Sources of GDP Forecast Errors
affiliations: University of Wisconsin - Milwaukee

detail.title: The Sources of GDP Forecast Errors
detail.abstract: Using Greenbook forecasts from 2001 to 2020, this paper decomposes Federal Reserve staff GDP forecast errors across expenditure components and horizons. Personal consumption accounts for the largest variance share at the nowcast but is relatively forecastable given its economic size. Net exports have nearly the same nowcast RMSE as consumption despite their much smaller net share of GDP. At longer horizons, business fixed investment and inventories become more important. Decomposing net exports reveals greater export-import error offset in turbulent than calm trade quarters, so an accurate net-export forecast need not imply accurate gross-flow forecasts.

title: From Sectors to Urban Nodes: A Functional-Morphological Zoning Dataset for Noida, India

detail.title: From Sectors to Urban Nodes: A Functional-Morphological Zoning Dataset for Noida, India
detail.abstract: Noida was planned and built through a sector system that remains indispensable for land administration, infrastructure and addressing. As the city matured, however, many of its employment, housing, market, education and transport systems came to operate across sector boundaries. This paper introduces version 1.0 of a functional-morphological zoning dataset that represents Noida at this intermediate urban scale. A zone is defined as a recognisable urban node: a contiguous or strongly connected territory whose different land uses participate in a common development history, employment-housing relationship, service system, built form and movement structure. Twelve top-level zones are identified, with further subzoning in certain cases. Six supplementary or peripheral polygons preserve river-edge, jurisdictional and morphologically exceptional land without forcing it into the node taxonomy. The complete 19-feature coverage spans 196.27 km 2 and contains no internal gaps, overlaps or invalid geometries. In addition to GeoPackage, GeoJSON and Shapefile layers, the release provides a sector crosswalk, adjacency table, village register, functionalanchor inventory, housing-form inventory, evidence register and zone-level OpenStreetMap figures. The resulting geography reveals Noida as a layered city of inherited industrial districts, mature residential and commercial centres, a sequence of Expressway nodes and a still-forming eastern frontier. It complements the official sector map while preserving it as the source geography.

title: National trends and territorial disparities in psychiatry residency fill rates in France: a longitudinal panel study, 2016–2026
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: National trends and territorial disparities in psychiatry residency fill rates in France: a longitudinal panel study, 2016–2026
detail.abstract: Background: Mental health needs are increasing across Europe, while psychiatric workforce planning in France is challenged by workforce ageing and territorial inequalities. Objective: To assess national trends in psychiatry residency fill rates in France and examine the territorial distribution of unfilled positions from 2016–2017 to 2025–2026. Methods: We conducted a nationwide retrospective longitudinal panel study including all 28 French residency subdivisions over 10 academic years. Opened and filled positions were extracted from decrees published in the French Official Journal. Fill rates were modelled using a beta-binomial generalised linear mixed model. Heterogeneity was quantified using the median odds ratio, and concentration using the Gini coefficient and top-share estimates. Results: The panel included 280 subdivision-year observations, corresponding to 5282 opened, 4719 filled, and 563 unfilled positions. Observed national fill rates declined from near-complete levels before 2019 to 82.49% in 2019–2020 and remained below pre-2019 levels thereafter. The model-based national fill rate decreased from 98.10% in the early period to 82.74% in the late period, an absolute change of -15.4 percentage points. Between-subdivision heterogeneity was substantial. Unfilled positions were territorially concentrated and the top 25% of subdivisions accounted for 61.3% of all unfilled positions. Conclusions: Psychiatry residency underfilling in France has become a sustained, territorially uneven workforce planning issue. In centralised rank-based allocation systems, workforce planning should monitor not only the number of training positions opened, but also their conversion into filled positions and the territorial accumulation of vacancies.

title: A Landslide but Not a Mandate: Putin's Re-Election & the Russo-Ukrainian War
affiliations: Charles University in Prague - Faculty of Law

detail.title: A Landslide but Not a Mandate: Putin's Re-Election & the Russo-Ukrainian War
detail.abstract: This paper measures dynamic beliefs about Vladimir Putin and the Russo-Ukrainian War surrounding the 2024 Russian presidential election. I leverage the staggered timing of the Panel Study of Russian Public Opinion and Attitudes (PROPA) survey in an event study design. I find roughly a 7.2 percentage point (p.p.) decline in two measures for Putin's approval and a 10.5 p.p. increase in trust towards Russians who fled the country following the 24 February 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Omitting strongly polarized responses (i.e., restricting the analysis to marginal responses on these issues), I find an 8.9 p.p. decline in trust towards federal television, a 7.2 p.p. increase in perceived likelihood of a new mobilization campaign (next 12 months), and a 12.6 p.p. decline in the perceived likelihood of a ceasefire (next 12 months). These short-run results suggest that Putin's landslide re-election should not be interpreted as a mandate for the continuation of his wartime policies.

title: The State of Electronification in 2026: From Venue Adoption to Workflow Automation in Global Fixed-income and Foreign-exchange Markets
affiliations: Imperial College London - Department of Mathematics

detail.title: The State of Electronification in 2026: From Venue Adoption to Workflow Automation in Global Fixed-income and Foreign-exchange Markets
detail.abstract: A decade after the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) described electronic trading as a steadily advancing transformation of fixed-income markets, the central empirical question has changed. The issue is no longer simply whether trading is electronic, but where further electronification is occurring, how it is measured, and whether the headline adoption rate has begun to flatten. This review revisits the 2016 BIS framework and reconstructs its cross-asset benchmark for 2012 and 2015. It then extends that benchmark with the latest defensible public indicators available by mid-2026, drawing on the 2025 BIS Triennial Central Bank Survey, ISDA SwapsInfo, Coalition Greenwich, official regulatory reports and recent market-microstructure research. The evidence supports a qualified slowdown thesis. In highly standardised markets, including futures, benchmark sovereign debt and the most liquid foreign-exchange products, the transition from voice to electronic execution is mature and incremental gains are constrained by saturation. In corporate credit, by contrast, adoption has continued to rise materially, with US investment-grade and high-yield electronic shares reaching approximately 48% and 32%, respectively, in 2025. The remaining non-electronic flow is increasingly selected: it is larger, less liquid, more bespoke, more information-sensitive and more dependent on dealer capital. At the same time, the most consequential developments have migrated beyond the binary electronic/voice distinction toward auto-quoting, algorithmic execution, portfolio trading, all-to-all protocols, data aggregation, consolidated tapes and central clearing. We therefore propose that electronification in 2026 should be measured as a multi-layer market-structure vector rather than a single execution-share statistic. The review concludes that electronification has slowed in its first-order extensive margin, but continues rapidly in its intensive margin: the composition, automation, connectivity and resilience of electronic markets.

title: Harm Reduction as Governance: An Integrated Decision Architecture for Policy, Recovery, and Health Systems
affiliations: University of Calgary

detail.title: Harm Reduction as Governance: An Integrated Decision Architecture for Policy, Recovery, and Health Systems
detail.abstract: Harm reduction implementation gaps in Canada and comparable jurisdictions are substantially associated with governance failures rather than evidence deficiencies. Core harm reduction interventions — opioid agonist therapy (OAT), naloxone distribution, needle and syringe programmes, and supervised consumption services — are supported by established evidence bases and endorsed by national guidelines, yet implementation across Canadian provinces and territories remains deeply inconsistent, with only two jurisdictions having stand-alone harm reduction policies as of the most recent comprehensive policy analysis.This paper proposes the Integrated Harm Reduction Systems Framework (IHRSF): a five-layer governance decision architecture for health authorities responsible for authorising, sustaining, and holding accountable harm reduction programmes. The IHRSF diagnoses governance failures across three dimensions (fragmentation, illegitimacy, invisibility) and six failure types, then addresses them through seven framework components, a twelve-step governance decision algorithm, and five mandatory accountability indicators.The framework is distinguished from existing approaches — including the Risk Environment Framework, Recovery-Oriented Systems of Care, and implementation science frameworks — by its operational function: it is designed to structure governance decisions prospectively, not to explain implementation variance retrospectively. Its accountability architecture requires a publicly maintained governance record that enables independent contestation of governance decisions. Five proposed accountability indicators — coverage rate, treatment linkage rate, equity-weighted mortality, community safety, and public reporting compliance — constitute the minimum governance performance standard.The IHRSF was derived through theoretically informed narrative synthesis across thirteen disciplinary domains. Its components and indicators are proposed standards that require prospective empirical validation. Five limitations are acknowledged: single-author synthesis, absence of prospective validation, Canadian primary context, the absence of Indigenous co-production in framework development, and the dependence of the accountability architecture on an independent review function external to the governance body.The IHRSF offers health authorities and policymakers a reproducible, transparent, and accountability-linked decision architecture for the governance of contested evidence-based interventions. Prospective application, independent evaluation, and co-production with people with lived and living experience of substance use are required to determine its effectiveness in practice.

title: The Open-Source Frontier AI Shock: Fear, Volatility, and the Repricing of Tech Giants (2025-2026)
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: The Open-Source Frontier AI Shock: Fear, Volatility, and the Repricing of Tech Giants (2025-2026)
