detail.abstract: This study examines how a series of open-source frontier artificial intelligence releases from Chinese laboratories shook financial markets between January 2025 and July 2026. We use event study methods and daily panel regressions to measure how high-tech and software stocks reacted to each announcement. Unlike past financial crises, where fear spread broadly across the entire market, the AI shock was highly concentrated. The ratio of tech volatility to broad market volatility (VXN/VIX) surged to 1.73, a level higher than during the 2008 Financial Crisis or the COVID-19 crash. This shows that investors were specifically worried about open-source AI disrupting proprietary software businesses, not about a general economic collapse. Options traders rushed to buy put options on tech stocks to hedge against further declines. On the announcement day of the Kimi K3 release, incumbent software companies experienced a cumulative abnormal return of-0.63%, confirming that markets view open-weight Chinese AI models as a threat to industry profits and future cash flows.

title: Adjusting the Hamilton Filter for One-Off Extraordinary Events

detail.title: Adjusting the Hamilton Filter for One-Off Extraordinary Events
detail.abstract: Hamilton's (2018) forecast-based filter can produce a mechanical, spurious cycle spike when an one-off extraordinary observation such as the onset of Covid-19 later enters its trend projection as a covariate. This paper introduces the Adjusted Hamilton (AH) filter, an intervention layer for the canonical Hamilton specification. AH retains the observed event when estimating its contemporaneous cycle while preventing its reuse as a later forecasting covariate; instead AH uses recursively constructed counterfactuals estimated from pre-event data. The resulting revision separates exactly into a global coefficient-estimation effect and a local covariate-replacement effect. Influence measures quantify the importance of the event designation, and a counterfactual diagnostic assesses whether AH improves forecasts at exposed dates. A U.S. GDP illustration and controlled simulations show the scope of the adjustment and the cost of false designation.

title: "Justice" by Deception: The Immigration Regime's Longstanding Reliance on Fraud and Coercion
affiliations: Seton Hall Law School

detail.title: "Justice" by Deception: The Immigration Regime's Longstanding Reliance on Fraud and Coercion
detail.abstract:
In Donald Trump’s America, ICE agents arbitrarily and violently arrest, detain, and deport immigrants without regard for their family ties, work history, benefit to the community, or military service.  Masked ICE agents make arrests when parents are dropping off children at school, attending court hearings or ICE check-ins, getting medical attention, or exercising their constitutionally protected right to free speech.  This dystopian reality is utterly terrifying, and it is reaching new heights, but it is not entirely new.  There is a long history of the courts and Congress countenancing, and condoning, ICE’s reliance on fraud and deception as enforcement tools.

For as long as the U.S. has been regulating our borders, immigration agents have been relying on fraud, deception, and coercion to enforce immigration laws; they have been masquerading as police to gain entrance to immigrants’ homes, and have been deceiving asylum seekers by telling them they would be reunited with children or taken to another state, when in reality they were being deported.  This Article explores why deception and coercion have long been countenanced in immigration matters, and how this has provided fertile ground for the mass weaponization of immigration enforcement against such a large segment of the population.  To do so, this Article analyzes the ever-increasing criminalization of immigration law and of immigrants.  Casting immigrants as criminals in the public mind laid the foundation for using the same types of tactics in immigration matters as in criminal interrogations where public safety is at risk.  But immigration regulation is civil, rather than criminal.  Significantly, this means that the same types of constitutional protections that apply in the criminal context, such as the right to appointed counsel, the right against self-incrimination, and the right not to be punished twice for same crime, do not apply to immigration regulation.

In addition to exploring the normative foundation for coercive tactics in immigration law that have provided the bedrock for the current massive deportation machine, this Article analyzes constitutional, state, and federal laws that should prohibit this type of action.  Prior to the second Trump Administration, immigrants rarely challenged ICE coercion and fraud through litigation.  But the heightened enforcement and detention and deportation of long-standing often lawfully present immigrants and citizens has resulted in greater legal challenges. This Article analyzes these challenges as well as legislative and regulatory actions aimed at prohibiting deceptive practices and coercion in immigration enforcement.

title: The Cognitive Friction of Money: Information-Theoretic Evaluation of a Fully Cashless Society

detail.title: The Cognitive Friction of Money: Information-Theoretic Evaluation of a Fully Cashless Society
detail.abstract: As digital transactions proliferate, public discourse often frames skepticism about cashless societies in terms of political concerns over state surveillance-such as the CBDC Anti-Surveillance State Act-while neglecting the underlying economic and psychological mechanisms. Setting aside these political dimensions, this paper employs Shannon entropy (H(X)) and Kullback-Leibler divergence (D KL (F ∥ G)) to rigorously evaluate the cognitive and macroeconomic consequences of monetary digitization. The results indicate that abstract digital interfaces attenuate loss aversion (λ eff → 1) and diminish the "pain of paying," thereby increasing money velocity (V T) and reducing liquidity preference (L(r, Y)). Empirical analysis challenges Rogoff's thesis, revealing only a weak correlation (R 2 = 0.2045) between cash use and shadow economy prevalence. To reconcile transactional efficiency with the need for cognitive discipline, this paper advocates a dual-layered approach: systematically phasing out high-denomination banknotes, legally protecting low-denomination cash ($1-$20), and mandating algorithmic UI/UX friction-including haptic cues, pre-transaction balance overlays, and unified liability dashboards-within digital payment ecosystems.

title: GLP-1 Treatment and Work Capacity
affiliations: ETH Zurich and

detail.title: GLP-1 Treatment and Work Capacity
detail.abstract: Using linked Finnish administrative records and a staggered difference-indifferences design, we estimate how starting semaglutide (Ozempic) affects work capacity, measured by medically certified sickness absence. The first purchase is followed by persistent use and improved glycemic control, indicating that recorded purchases correspond to sustained and clinically active treatment. The reduction in sickness absence is near zero during months 0-5, becomes progressively larger thereafter, and is largest during months 12-18. Averaged over event months 0-18, sickness allowance receipt falls by 16.9 percent and compensated days by 14.3 percent relative to pre-treatment means. The decline in full-day sickness absence is not offset by greater reliance on unemployment or partial sickness benefits. The results show that semaglutide improves work capacity and can generate economic benefits beyond its direct effects on metabolic health.

title: The Shape of Care: Planning for Telemedicine Rollout under Heterogeneous Adoption
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania, University of Pennsylvania, University of Pennsylvania, Pennsylvania State University and University of Pennsylvania - Department of Biostatistics, Epidemiology, and Informatics

detail.title: The Shape of Care: Planning for Telemedicine Rollout under Heterogeneous Adoption
detail.abstract: When a multi-hospital health system expands telemedicine, managers must decide, hospital by hospital and specialty by specialty, whether expansion will require changes to downstream capacity such as staffing, scheduling, and follow-up appointments. This decision is challenging because telemedicine adoption is uneven across hospitals, leaving many rollout targets with little or no local data, and because average downstream utilization masks the pathway-level changes that determine downstream capacity needs. We develop a multitask K-modal regression framework that forecasts, for each hospitalspecialty cell, how telemedicine rollout would change 90-day downstream charges. The framework decomposes downstream charges into pathway membership and the typical charge within each pathway, and borrows information across hospitals within the same specialty through a shared low-rank structure, thereby enabling prediction for hospitals with little or no telemedicine adoption. We establish finite-sample guarantees that quantify the benefits of information sharing while accounting for bias from hospital heterogeneity. Applying the framework to the University of Pennsylvania Health System across four hospitals and nine specialties, we obtain three managerial findings. First, rollout effects are highly concentrated: for eight of the nine specialties, expanding telemedicine to the highest observed adoption level leaves downstream care pathways largely unchanged. Second, Psychiatry is the primary exception, with lowadoption hospitals exhibiting substantial increases in the typical charge of the follow-up pathway. Third, leave-one-out validation accurately reconstructs follow-up pathway intensity when local telemedicine variation is removed, supporting planning for hospitals with no prior telemedicine adoption.

title: Unequal Burdens: Female Labor Force Participation and Informality in the Global North and South During the 2019-2024 Polycrisis

detail.title: Unequal Burdens: Female Labor Force Participation and Informality in the Global North and South During the 2019-2024 Polycrisis
detail.abstract:
Abstract

The 2019–2024 polycrisis—including the COVID-19 pandemic, inflationary pressures, supply chain disruptions, and climate-related shocks—has reshaped female labor market outcomes across the world. This study investigates whether these crises generated divergent labor market responses in the Global North and the Global South by comparing the "She-cession" hypothesis with the "Distress Sale of Labor" hypothesis. Using harmonized labor market data from the International Labour Organization (ILO) and the World Bank, the analysis focuses on Germany, France, India, Brazil, and South Africa over the period 2019–2024.

The study employs descriptive analysis, Pearson's correlation, Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression, and paired sample t-tests to examine changes in female labor force participation, unemployment, and informal employment. The findings reveal a clear divergence. In the Global North, rising unemployment significantly reduced female labor force participation, supporting the She-cession hypothesis. In contrast, the Global South experienced a statistically significant increase in female labor force participation during the recovery period; however, this increase was accompanied by persistently high levels of informal employment, indicating a distress-driven expansion of labor supply rather than improved economic empowerment.

The results demonstrate that post-pandemic labor market recovery differed not only in magnitude but also in quality. While the Global North faced a temporary crisis of labor force participation linked to care constraints, the Global South experienced a structural increase in precarious and informal employment. These findings highlight the limitations of evaluating women's economic progress solely through participation rates and emphasize the need to incorporate employment quality into policy assessment. The paper recommends region-specific policy interventions, including strengthened childcare infrastructure in advanced economies and expanded social protection and income security measures in developing economies.

Keywords: Female Labor Force Participation; She-cession; Distress Sale of Labor; Informal Employment; Global North; Global South; Gender Inequality; COVID-19; Polycrisis; Development Economics; OLS Regression.

title: The Value of Behavioral Policies
affiliations: University of Chicago - Department of Economics, Bocconi University, Australian National University (ANU) and Washington University in St. Louis

detail.title: The Value of Behavioral Policies
detail.abstract: Behavioral interventions have become central to modern public policy, but their empirical promise remains contested because estimated treatment effects often appear small. We argue that a policy response is economically meaningful only relative to the response generated by alternative policies. We assemble more than 1,200 estimates from over 600 studies comparing "nudges" and traditional price interventions in the markets for cigarettes, alcohol, influenza vaccination, electricity, and residential water. Translating nudge effects into equivalent price changes, we find that behavioral interventions often correspond to enormous fiscal interventions, from an 11% tax on electricity to a 100% subsidy on influenza vaccinations. Nudges are also more cost-effective than price instruments in all markets, but cost-effectiveness does not predict the welfare ranking of policies. Using a behavioral extension of the Marginal Value of Public Funds, we show that nudges have high welfare returns at the margin, while price instruments often generate larger total surplus at scale.

title: Bridging the distance: Evaluating Chile's Institutional and Digital Competitiveness in the Era of U.S. Strategic Shoring

detail.title: Bridging the distance: Evaluating Chile's Institutional and Digital Competitiveness in the Era of U.S. Strategic Shoring

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: The disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and the escalation of U.S.-China trade tensions revealed structural vulnerabilities in global supply chains that had been optimized primarily for cost efficiency. In response, the concept of strategic shoring emerged as a framework for relocating supply chain operations toward countries that share institutional and democratic standards with the United States (Savoy, 2023). This paper evaluates Chile's potential as a destination within that framework, focusing on three dimensions: democratic stability and rule of law, the bilateral Free Trade Agreement in force since 2004, and digital infrastructure. While Chile's geographic distance from the United States-approximately 8,500 kilometers-presents a clear disadvantage for goods-based trade, the analysis suggests that for high-value service operations, institutional reliability and digital connectivity may outweigh physical proximity. The paper also examines Chile's limitations, including its small domestic market, unresolved social tensions, and vulnerability to shifts in U.S. policy priorities.

title: When Political Uncertainty Mimics Efficiency under the Adaptive Markets Hypothesis: Peru as a Rare Case Today, a Precedent for Tomorrow?

detail.title: When Political Uncertainty Mimics Efficiency under the Adaptive Markets Hypothesis: Peru as a Rare Case Today, a Precedent for Tomorrow?
detail.abstract: This paper examines how extreme domestic political uncertainty disrupts expectation formation in the Peruvian stock market, causing market dynamics to appear as statistical efficiency-lower return predictability-rather than the temporary inefficiency predicted by the standard Adaptive Markets Hypothesis. Using weekly data from 1990 to 2026, the study applies parametric and nonparametric rolling variance ratio tests to compare global shocks and domestic political events, supported by fractional logit regressions for the latter. The evidence reveals a sharp asymmetry. Global crises, such as the Great Recession and the COVID-19 pandemic, generate temporary return predictability, consistent with investors relying on imperfect heuristics before adapting. By contrast, domestic political shocks produce the opposite pattern. Elections involving radical or outsider candidates and episodes of institutional crisis reduce return predictability, moving the market toward statistical efficiency. This does not indicate better information processing, but a breakdown in expectation formation under extreme regime uncertainty. Comparative evidence from Latin America suggests that Peru's party-system collapse and weak institutionalization explain this distinctive response. The paper shows that institutional fragility can reshape, and even invert, standard adaptive-market dynamics.

title: Robust Currency Cointegration using Bayesian Optimization
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Singapore Management University, Singapore University of Social Sciences and Singapore Management University - Lee Kong Chian School of Business

detail.title: Robust Currency Cointegration using Bayesian Optimization
detail.abstract: Traditional econometric methods for cointegration analysis like the Johansen test are optimized for in-sample performance.  For portfolio managers, this often yields fragile,  unstable solutions, leading to high turnover and volatile out-of-sample performance. This paper reframes the portfolio approach as a Bayesian optimization (BO) problem, shifting the objective from in-sample statistical significance to out-of-sample portfolio stability and tradability.  By optimizing a dual-objective function that balances statistical stationarity with economically meaningful variation, the BO framework identifies globally robust cointegrating vectors.  Empirical analysis on G10 currencies from 2010 to 2024 demonstrates that BO portfolios exhibit substantially more stable cointegrating weights, leading to significantly lower portfolio turnover and better risk-adjusted returns compared to traditional benchmarks.  These results offer a resilient blueprint for practitioners seeking to integrate machine learning with classical econometrics to build durable trading strategies.

title: Lex Doctrina: The Doctrinal Floor for Artificial Intelligence Competence in U.S. Legal Education
affiliations: New York Law School

detail.title: Lex Doctrina: The Doctrinal Floor for Artificial Intelligence Competence in U.S. Legal Education
detail.abstract:
Legal education has treated the integration of artificial intelligence into the curriculum as a matter of institutional discretion. This Article argues that framing is wrong and has been wrong since a specific date. ABA Accreditation Standard 301, Model Rule of Professional Conduct 1.1 Comment 8, and ABA Formal Opinion 512, issued July 29, 2024, together establish a doctrinal floor: a binding obligation, already in force, that accredited American law schools teach the competence to use generative artificial intelligence tools without compromising the duty of independent verification that now governs their use in practice.

The Article's method is conservative. It proposes no new rule. It shows that existing instruments, read together as courts and regulators already read them, compel a conclusion the academy has not yet drawn. It draws that conclusion from three converging bodies of evidence: an empirical record showing legal hallucination rates as high as eighty-eight percent in general-purpose models; a rapidly accumulating case law record running from Mata v. Avianca through a 2026 Quebec Superior Court decision annulling an arbitral award for an arbitrator's undisclosed delegation of judgment; and a parallel architecture of state regulation in California, New York, and Florida that is already defining what technological competence requires. Drawing on the Carnegie Foundation's three apprenticeships and the MacCrate Report's statement of lawyering skills and values, the Article translates the doctrinal floor into a model competence standard organized around three categories of AI use, distinguished by their relationship to the formation of professional judgment.

The question facing law schools is not whether to adapt their curricula to artificial intelligence. It is how quickly they can implement an obligation that has already attached.

title: Estimating a Process of Health Formation in Older Adults: The Roles of Physical Functioning, Cognition, and Mental Health
affiliations: SUNY at Stony Brook University, College of Arts and Science, Department of Economics and State University of New York (SUNY), Stony Brook

detail.title: Estimating a Process of Health Formation in Older Adults: The Roles of Physical Functioning, Cognition, and Mental Health
detail.abstract: Health in older adults evolves along multiple, interdependent dimensions. This paper develops and estimates a dynamic model of health formation that distinguishes physical, cognitive, and mental domains. The model is estimated using a comprehensive set of health measures from the Health and Retirement Study. The results reveal novel patterns of complementarity across the health domains. Physical health plays a central role, serving as a significant determinant of mental health as well as of employment, health investment, and mortality. Mental health is an important determinant of employment and mortality, but it is found to be more transitory and to have little feedback on the other health domains. The model is used to identify the periods in which targeted health domains have the largest impacts and generate the greatest spillovers across domains. Finally, we map the latent domains to commonly used measures such as self-reported health, clarifying which aspects of health drive variation in these widely used indicators.

title: Two Selection Problems, One Bias Term: Experimental Sign-Up Is Treatment Choice in Disguise
affiliations: University of Chicago - Department of Economics

detail.title: Two Selection Problems, One Bias Term: Experimental Sign-Up Is Treatment Choice in Disguise
detail.abstract: Consider a referee report containing the sentence: "Assignment to treatment was voluntary, though the authors acknowledge this as a limitation in the conclusion." The Editor would summarily reject. Now replace "assignment to treatment" with "entry into the experimental sample," and the sentence describes the modal published experiment. This study shows that both biases are the same mathematical object. The bias from non-random sample entry is the sorting-on-gains term from the classic selection decomposition. Interestingly, they both admit an isomorphic Roy micro-foundation and inverse-Mills characterization. A simple calibration reveals that for the typical experiment, the observed bias can be large. One solution to this bias is to conduct a natural field experiment (NFE). When an NFE is not possible, three alternative reporting practices are offered.

title: Hierarchical PANI@Cu₀.₉₅V₂O₅@Carbon Cloth Composites Enabling Self-Powered Flexible Multimodal Sensing for Parkinsonian Handwriting Recognition
affiliations: Hebei University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Hebei University, Hebei University, Hebei University, Hebei University and Hebei University

detail.title: Hierarchical PANI@Cu₀.₉₅V₂O₅@Carbon Cloth Composites Enabling Self-Powered Flexible Multimodal Sensing for Parkinsonian Handwriting Recognition
detail.abstract: Flexible electronic technology is rapidly advancing toward intelligence, self-powering, and multi-scenario adaptability. However, critical bottlenecks remain unresolved: most functional materials possess a single performance and thus fail to simultaneously realize sensing and energy storage capabilities. Herein, flexible carbon cloth (CC) was employed as the substrate to successfully construct PANI@Cu0.95V₂O₅@CC composite electrode materials, which feature a hierarchical polyaniline (PANI) coating architecture, via a synergistic combination of hydrothermal synthesis and electrodeposition coating techniques. Performance characterization reveals that the pressure sensor delivers an ultrahigh sensitivity of 1.2 × 10⁴ kPa⁻¹, a broad pressure detection range spanning 0–200 kPa, remarkable durability over 8000 cycles, and a fast, consistent response and recovery time of 83 ms. The gas sensor, in turn, enables accurate detection of ethanol at concentrations from 1 to 100 ppm. Meanwhile, the photoelectric sensor exhibits superior performance in the visible spectrum, with its photocurrent varying from 10 to 100 mW·cm-2. Furthermore, the PCC-derived zinc-ion battery achieves a specific capacity peak of 231 mAh·g-1, retaining 90% of its initial capacity after 2000 charge–discharge cycles. The pressure sensor was integrated with the zinc-ion battery, and a self-powered sensing system was constructed by incorporating deep learning algorithms, which achieved accurate recognition of handwritten strokes between healthy individuals and patients with Parkinson’s disease. This work provides a novel approach for the design and preparation of multifunctional composite materials, and also opens up a new technical pathway for the development of self-powered wearable electronic devices.

title: Deep Learning for Stenosis Assessment and Intraplaque Neovascularization Grading in Carotid Artery Using Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasound Video
affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Shanghai General Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU), Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Shanghai General Hospital and

detail.title: Deep Learning for Stenosis Assessment and Intraplaque Neovascularization Grading in Carotid Artery Using Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasound Video

detail.abstract:
Background: Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) enables noninvasive carotid stenosis assessment and intraplaque neovascularization (IPN) grading for evaluating plaque vulnerability and stroke risk, but manual interpretation is time-consuming and expertise-dependent. We aimed to develop a deep learning (DL)-based automated method for stenosis assessment and IPN grading of carotid plaque from CEUS videos and to compare its performance with that of experienced radiologists.

Methods: This multi-center study retrospectively collected CEUS videos from three tertiary hospitals between June 2019 and August 2023 and divided them into training and validation sets. An independent test set was retrospectively collected at XXX Hospital from January to December 2023. Stenosis degree was classified as mild (<50%), moderate (50%-70%), and severe (³70%), with CTA as the reference (n = 152). Ground-truth IPN grades were primarily established through consensus between two senior radiologists, with disagreements resolved by an arbitrator. All radiologists and the arbitrator were blinded to patient information. Performance metrics included the Dice coefficient, expected average overlap, accuracy, and weighted k coefficient.

Findings: For three-class stenosis classification, the model achieved 96% accuracy (95% CI: 91%–99%) and weighted k = 0.87 (95% CI: 0.76–0.97), demonstrating strong concordance with CTA. For binary classification at the clinically significant threshold, performance improved to 98% accuracy (95% CI: 94%–99%) and weighted k = 0.93 (95% CI: 0.85–1.00), highlighting its clinical utility. For IPN grading, accuracies of 88% (95% CI: 81%–94%) and 84% (95% CI: 79%–87%) were achieved in the validation and independent test sets, respectively, indicating good generalizability. Compared with radiologists, the model increased efficiency more than 100-fold for stenosis assessment and ~2000-fold for IPN grading.

Interpretation: The proposed DL framework enables accurate, consistent, and highly efficient stenosis assessment and IPN grading from CEUS videos, demonstrating radiologist-level performance and facilitating early screening in high-risk populations.

title: Critical Event Governance Review (CEGR) A Retrospective Governance Documentation Standard for AI-Supported Justice Environments
affiliations: Indiana University, Indianapolis - Indiana University Indianapolis and Indiana University, Indianapolis - Indiana University Indianapolis

detail.title: Critical Event Governance Review (CEGR) A Retrospective Governance Documentation Standard for AI-Supported Justice Environments
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly integrated into justice-sector operations, influencing institutional decision-making across corrections, courts, community supervision, law enforcement, and other public safety organizations. Contemporary AI governance frameworks have substantially strengthened responsible deployment by emphasizing transparency, accountability, lifecycle risk management, human oversight, and technical assurance. Comparatively less attention, however, has been devoted to documenting and reconstructing the organizational decision environments surrounding consequential events after deployment has occurred.
This paper introduces Critical Event Governance Review (CEGR) as a retrospective governance documentation standard situated within the broader conceptual architecture of Justice Decision Observability (JDO). Rather than functioning as a technical audit, administrative investigation, legal review, or compliance assessment, CEGR documents the operational decision environment surrounding consequential events to improve institutional understanding of how organizational authority, practitioner discretion, operational conditions, available information, and AI-supported outputs collectively influenced decision formation.
The paper argues that retrospective governance documentation represents a distinct governance capability that complements existing AI governance frameworks without replacing them. Whereas technical governance seeks to explain how AI systems functioned, governance reconstruction seeks to explain the institutional environments within which technological information became organizational action. By distinguishing governance reconstruction from fault determination, technical assessment, and organizational investigation, the paper expands contemporary discussions of AI governance to include retrospective documentation of operational decision environments as an independent object of governance inquiry. 
The framework presented is conceptual rather than procedural. It is intended to contribute to governance scholarship by advancing retrospective governance documentation as a complementary component of responsible AI governance while deliberately avoiding disclosure of proprietary implementation methodologies.

title:
The Decision that Looked Reasonable at the Time 
Hindsight, Operational Judgement, and Institutional Reconstruction Failure in AI-Supported Justice Environments Conceptual Foundations, Scope, and Implications for AI Governance
affiliations: Indiana University, Indianapolis - Indiana University Indianapolis and Indiana University, Indianapolis - Indiana University Indianapolis

detail.title:
The Decision that Looked Reasonable at the Time 
Hindsight, Operational Judgement, and Institutional Reconstruction Failure in AI-Supported Justice Environments Conceptual Foundations, Scope, and Implications for AI Governance
detail.abstract: Justice and public safety agencies increasingly rely on artificial intelligence (AI)-supported technologies, predictive analytics, automated alerts, and integrated decision-support systems to inform operational activities across corrections, community supervision, courts, detention, and other high-consequence environments. While existing governance frameworks largely emphasize technical explainability, algorithmic transparency, regulatory compliance, and system performance, comparatively little attention has been directed toward how human operational decisions are retrospectively reconstructed and evaluated after critical events occur. This paper argues that a significant governance challenge exists when post-incident institutional reviews assess historical decisions using levels of information, temporal clarity, and outcome awareness that were unavailable to frontline personnel at the time authority was exercised. Building upon established research in hindsight bias, naturalistic decision making, bounded rationality, organizational accidents, and sensemaking, this paper introduces Hindsight Governance Distortion as an execution-layer governance concept describing the institutional tendency to reinterpret operational judgment through retrospective certainty rather than real-time ambiguity. The paper further advances the concept of Reconstruction Asymmetry, describing the imbalance between the fragmented operational conditions experienced by decision-makers and the expanded visibility available during post-incident review. Together, these concepts expand the theoretical foundations of Justice Decision Observability (JDO) by demonstrating that governance maturity depends not only on reconstructing what occurred, but also on accurately reconstructing the operational conditions under which authority originally formed. The paper argues that distinguishing real-time operational judgment from retrospective interpretation is essential for institutional accountability, organizational learning, defensible governance, and responsible oversight within AI-supported justice environments. As AI continues to reshape operational workflows, execution-layer governance must increasingly account for the human decision environment that exists between technological outputs and institutional outcomes.

detail.title: The Constraint Gap: Rational Underutilization and the Limits of Digital Adoption in African Micro-Enterprises

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Informed consent was obtained from all individual enterprise owners/operators participating in the study. All procedures were conducted in accordance with standard academic ethical practices for research involving human participants
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Why does the rapid diffusion of digital technologies in Africa yield such modest productivity gains for micro-enterprises? This paper identifies and formalizes the constraint gap-the wedge between technology adoption and intensive utilization-as the central explanation. Using original firm-level survey data from 87 owner-managed micro-enterprises in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, the paper shows that while 92 percent of firms adopt at least one digital technology, only 21 percent use these tools intensively across core business functions. This divergence is not driven by lack of awareness or negative attitudes, but by rational underutilization under binding financial, human capital, infrastructural, and institutional constraints. Utilization intensity declines sharply as constraints bundle, and utilization-rather than adoption-is strongly associated with reported improvements in profits, client reach, and operational efficiency. By reframing post-adoption behavior as a constrained optimization problem, the paper shifts analytical and policy attention from adoption barriers to the feasibility of intensive use, with implications for digitalization strategies targeting micro-enterprise productivity. The analysis is deliberately diagnostic rather than causal, positioning utilization intensity as a core measurement gap in digital development research.

title:
The Governance Gap Between Policy and Practice
Why Operational Reality Rarely Aligns With Institutional Procedure
affiliations: Indiana University, Indianapolis - Indiana University Indianapolis and Indiana University, Indianapolis - Indiana University Indianapolis

detail.title:
The Governance Gap Between Policy and Practice
Why Operational Reality Rarely Aligns With Institutional Procedure
detail.abstract:
Justice and public safety organizations rely upon policies, procedures, governance frameworks, and technological systems to establish expectations for institutional decision-making. These formal governance structures define how operational activities are intended to occur; however, they often provide only limited visibility into how decisions actually develop once they enter dynamic operational environments. Personnel routinely exercise judgment under conditions shaped by competing priorities, organizational pressures, incomplete information, staffing realities, and increasing reliance on AI-supported technologies. Consequently, operational practice may diverge from documented institutional procedure in ways that remain largely invisible until a significant event exposes underlying governance conditions.

This paper examines the governance gap between policy and practice as an execution-layer governance challenge rather than solely a matter of compliance, procedural adherence, or technological performance. Drawing upon organizational learning, bounded rationality, street-level bureaucracy, human factors, and institutional governance literature, the paper argues that written policy alone cannot fully explain how consequential decisions are interpreted, adapted, prioritized, and operationalized under real-world conditions. The discussion introduces the Decision Visibility Gap as a conceptual governance construct describing the limited visibility institutions often possess regarding the operational conditions surrounding human decision-making after governance structures enter live operational environments.

title: ERP-Based Data Integration Framework for Business Operations and Managerial Decision Support
affiliations: Lamar University

detail.title: ERP-Based Data Integration Framework for Business Operations and Managerial Decision Support
detail.abstract: Modern organizations rely on enterprise resource planning systems to coordinate financial operations, procurement activities, customer management, and internal reporting processes. However, many organizations face difficulties when operational data remains distributed across different departments and software platforms. This study presents an ERP-based data integration framework that consolidates operational datasets and supports managerial decision-making. The research examines the use of enterprise systems such as SAP to integrate financial records, customer relationship management data, and operational reporting information. The proposed framework introduces structured data pipelines, automated reporting procedures, and dashboard-based visualization for monitoring business activities. The system allows managers to review sales trends, operational performance indicators, and financial summaries within a centralized reporting interface. Case analysis demonstrates that ERP-based integration improves reporting accuracy, reduces manual processing time, and supports timely decision-making across departments. The findings show that structured enterprise data systems improve organizational transparency and operational coordination. The proposed framework further demonstrates scalability and practical applicability for modern enterprise environments.

title:
Justice Decision Observability (JDO)
Defining the Foundational Governance Discipline for Execution-Layer Decision Environments (v2.0)
affiliations: Indiana University, Indianapolis - Indiana University Indianapolis and Indiana University, Indianapolis - Indiana University Indianapolis

detail.title:
Justice Decision Observability (JDO)
Defining the Foundational Governance Discipline for Execution-Layer Decision Environments (v2.0)
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence, predictive analytics, automated alerts, and digitally mediated decision-support systems are rapidly transforming operational decision-making across justice and public safety institutions. Existing governance frameworks have largely focused on policy development, regulatory compliance, algorithmic accountability, procurement oversight, technical validation, and ethical principles governing the design and deployment of AI-enabled systems. There has been less attention directed toward the operational environment in which human decision-makers interpret technological information, exercise professional judgment, and translate institutional authority into consequential action.

This publication defines Justice Decision Observability (JDO) as a foundational governance discipline dedicated to understanding execution-layer decision environments. Rather than evaluating technological performance or institutional compliance alone, JDO establishes a conceptual framework for examining how human decisions develop after governance structures, organizational policies, and technological systems enter live operational use. The paper introduces the foundational principles of the discipline, defines its conceptual boundaries, explains its relationship to existing governance frameworks, and identifies several core concepts, including the Execution Layer, Decision Visibility Gap, and Moment of Authority that together provide a governance perspective for understanding operational decision-making in AI-supported environments.

Drawing upon scholarship in organizational theory, decision science, human factors, public administration, and AI governance, this publication argues that governance maturity depends not only upon the quality of institutional policies and technological systems but also upon understanding how those systems function during real-world operations. The publication is conceptual and doctrinal in nature. It intentionally excludes proprietary methodologies, implementation procedures, governance instrumentation, reconstruction protocols, scoring systems, software architecture, and operational frameworks developed by Justice Beacon Solutions. As the foundational authority publication within the Justice Decision Observability Canon, this paper establishes the theoretical basis for a governance discipline intended to advance institutional accountability, operational understanding, and execution-layer governance within increasingly AI-supported justice environments.

title: The Missing System Theorem: The Limits of Welfare Recovery from Payoff-Space Information

detail.title: The Missing System Theorem: The Limits of Welfare Recovery from Payoff-Space Information

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Erik Postnieks is the founder of the Center for Decision Accounting and developer of the research program examined in this paper. He received no external funding for this study and declares no other personal or financial relationships that could have influenced the work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This theoretical study involved no human participants, patient data, interventions, or identifiable private information. Ethics approval and informed consent were therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was self-funded by the author and received no external financial support.

detail.abstract: Modern disasters often begin as transactions that look successful. Mortgage securitization generated profits while fragility accumulated; carbon-intensive production generated income while destabilizing the climate; plastics and antibiotic use produced gains while degrading health, ecosystems, and essential medicines. They share a structure: the transaction's parties gain while the system supporting them loses. This paper proves why payoff analysis can miss that loss. The Missing System Theorem establishes that when two situations give all represented parties the same payoffs but produce different system welfare, no method using only those payoffs can distinguish them. The antibiotic witness makes the failure concrete. In Scenario A, treatment cures the current patient without increasing resistance in the affected population. In Scenario B, the same prescription produces the same cure and payment but helps resistant bacteria survive and spread, making antibiotics less effective for future patients. The paper calls the resulting outcome a Hollow Win: a win in every represented account and a loss for the surrounding system. The theorem anchors a public program spanning the 61 studies listed in Appendix C-including four comparison controls-and a 190-country reform grid. The System Asset Pricing Model (SAPM) measures annual system-welfare loss against industry revenue; Decision Accounting records the missing consequence before approval; Changing the Game connects the record to a rule that can alter conduct; and a system-welfare contra account places the loss beside gross domestic product (GDP). The result shows why apparent progress can conceal decline and how society can stop rewarding Hollow Wins.

title: Accountable Inference Reputation Protocol (AIRP) An Advocate for AI Users and a Surface for Policy Implementation

detail.title: Accountable Inference Reputation Protocol (AIRP) An Advocate for AI Users and a Surface for Policy Implementation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has filed a United States provisional patent application covering client-side implementation mechanisms described in this paper. The protocol, the architecture, and the methods described are deliberately not covered by that filing and are dedicated to open use under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0; the reference implementation is released under the Apache License 2.0. The author intends to develop commercial applications of the described architecture and therefore has a financial interest in its adoption. The author has no relationship, financial or otherwise, with any AI model provider, regulator, or advocacy organization discussed in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a conceptual and legal analysis involving no human subjects, patients, or participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no funding. The author is unaffiliated and conducted the work independently.

detail.abstract:
Every conversation a person has with an AI model passes through software on their own screen. In current consumer deployments that software is built and operated by the company that trained the model, so the only component positioned to hold a duty to the user answers instead to the party the user may need protection from. Other technologies of comparable potency resolved this by interposing a party whose loyalty runs the other way: the pharmacist, the broker, the browser. This paper specifies one for artificial intelligence. An inference advocate is an independently operated client bound by an enacted duty of loyalty to the user alone, operating under the Accountable Inference Reputation Protocol (AIRP). The protocol establishes which model produced a given response, confirms the endpoint was authorized to serve it, evaluates the response independently, gates delivery according to the provider's accumulated conduct and the user's own jurisdiction, and reports incident rates without reporting content. The user's interaction history stays on their own device, and the few facts enforcement needs about them are proven without revealing who they are. Almost none of this requires invention. The machinery is borrowed from internet protocols we already know how to build and run at scale, so the engineering is tractable and the cost is modest. Two elements have no developed precedent: enforcing provider conduct by aggregate incident rate rather than case-by-case adjudication, and applying the user's own jurisdiction at the point of delivery. The need is already documented in law. Four jurisdictions have prohibited sycophancy, engineered emotional dependence, and engagement optimization that overrides a system's own safety behavior, while other instruments mandate machine-readable provenance and independent auditing. Every one of these obligations describes something that has to be observed where a response reaches a person, and every one leaves the observing to the party being observed. Nobody is watching on the user's behalf. This paper defines that role, places it at the boundary where a response reaches a person, and sets out how to keep it from being captured. The aim is plain enough: the software on your screen should work for you.

Previously circulated as the Accountable Inference Delivery Protocol (AIDP). The protocol, the architecture, and the argument are unchanged; only the name has been revised.

title: Does Digital Orientation Drive ESG Performance: A Cross-Sector Analysis of Indian Listed Companies (NIFTY 500, FY2023-24)

detail.title: Does Digital Orientation Drive ESG Performance: A Cross-Sector Analysis of Indian Listed Companies (NIFTY 500, FY2023-24)
detail.abstract: This study examines whether a company's Digital Orientation (DO) measured across four dimensions adapted from Kindermann et al. (2021) significantly predicts its Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) performance among Nifty 500 companies for fiscal year 2023-24. Using a computer aided text analysis (CATA) methodology applied to annual reports and CRISIL ESG ratings, the analysis covers 437 companies with both valid DO Scores and ESG Ratings. Our findings reveal that while digital orientation shows a small statistically significant positive correlation with ESG performance in unadjusted analysis (r = 0.123, p = 0.010), this relationship disappears entirely once industry fixed effects are controlled for (β = 0.043, p = 0.353). Among the four digital orientation dimensions, only Digital Architecture Configuration retains a significant independent association with ESG rating (β = 0.0032, p = 0.0008). Sector level analysis reveals that only Capital Goods exhibits a statistically significant positive DO-ESG relationship (r = 0.384, p = 0.005), while Information Technology despite being the most digitally intensive sector shows no correlation whatsoever (r =-0.023, p = 0.916). Divergence quadrant analysis further reveals that high digital/ low ESG companies cluster in Chemicals and Capital Goods, contradicting the hypothesis that digitally native service sectors would dominate this quadrant. Overall, the evidence favors the interpretation that digital adoption and ESG performance are largely independent, industry driven phenomena rather than causally linked outcomes with a narrow exception for infrastructure specific digital investment.

title: The Life and Times of Blockchain Ventures: Innovation, Vulnerability, and Survival
affiliations: University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management

detail.title: The Life and Times of Blockchain Ventures: Innovation, Vulnerability, and Survival
detail.abstract: Blockchain ventures exhibit failure rates markedly higher than those of conventional startups, yet the technological drivers of their survival remain underexplored. This study examines how innovation and security risk shape the long-term survival of blockchain ventures. Drawing on detailed source code data from blockchain ventures' GitHub repositories, together with corresponding survival and market data, I employ two code-based metrics, code originality and code vulnerability, and estimate their effects on venture survival using Cox proportional hazards and Weibull accelerated failure time models. The results reveal a two-sided dynamic: higher code originality decreases failure risk through an appropriability channel, whereas greater code vulnerability increases failure risk through a legitimacy channel. Further analyses reveal that these effects are heterogeneous across venture development profiles. Originality reduces failure risk for pioneering ventures but increases it for imitative ventures, while vulnerability raises failure risk for both groups, with a substantially stronger effect among imitative ventures. Overall, this study links code-level technological characteristics to venture survival and highlights that effective survival strategies should align with a venture's development profile.

title: From Adoption to Intimacy: Experiential and Emotional Pathways of Digital Customer Intimacy in FinTech
affiliations: , University of Southern Queensland, University of Southern Queensland and University of Southern Queensland

detail.title: From Adoption to Intimacy: Experiential and Emotional Pathways of Digital Customer Intimacy in FinTech
detail.abstract: This study examines how user relationships with FinTech platforms evolve beyond initial adoption, focusing on the formation of Digital Customer Intimacy (DCI) in human–machine interactions. Using a quantitative-dominant design combining survey data from 414 users and thematic analysis of open-ended responses, the study develops and tests a staged-based model linking cognitive evaluations, experiential interaction, emotional connection, and Digital Customer Intimacy (DCI). The findings show that while perceived quality and behavioural intention explain early engagement, emotional connection is the most direct driver of digital intimacy. Trust supports engagement but influences intimacy only indirectly through emotional pathways. By introducing and validating DCI as a distinct relational construct, the study extends digital service research beyond behavioural continuance toward an understanding of how emotionally meaningful interactions shape long-term digital relationships.

title: Justice Decision Observability (JDO)-Understanding the Discipline: What It Is, What It Is Not, and Why The Justice Ecosystem Needs It (v2.0)
affiliations: Indiana University, Indianapolis - Indiana University Indianapolis and Indiana University, Indianapolis - Indiana University Indianapolis

detail.title: Justice Decision Observability (JDO)-Understanding the Discipline: What It Is, What It Is Not, and Why The Justice Ecosystem Needs It (v2.0)
detail.abstract:
Justice and public safety organizations increasingly operate within environments shaped by artificial intelligence, automated monitoring systems, predictive technologies, digital workflows, institutional policies, and expanding expectations regarding accountability. Existing governance frameworks have significantly strengthened oversight of technology, compliance, organizational controls, and institutional outcomes. Comparatively less attention, however, has been directed toward understanding the operational environments in which human decisions are formed after these governance systems enter live institutional use.

This publication provides an institutional introduction to Justice Decision Observability (JDO) as a governance discipline dedicated to understanding execution-layer decision environments. Rather than evaluating technological performance, legal compliance, or organizational legitimacy, JDO establishes a conceptual framework for understanding the operational conditions under which institutional authority is exercised. The paper explains what Justice Decision Observability is, clarifies what it is not, examines the concept of the Decision Visibility Gap, and discusses why execution-layer governance represents an increasingly important dimension of institutional accountability within AI-supported justice systems.

Drawing upon scholarship in organizational learning, public administration, human factors, decision science, and AI governance, this publication argues that meaningful institutional understanding extends beyond policies, systems, and outcomes to include the operational environments in which human judgment transforms information into institutional action.

title: Beyond the Black-Box Cloud: How Liquid AI Fits the Operational and Ethical Realities of Health and Social Care
affiliations: Dignity Alliance Massachusetts

detail.title: Beyond the Black-Box Cloud: How Liquid AI Fits the Operational and Ethical Realities of Health and Social Care

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No outside interests
declarations.ethicsApproval: None required
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract: The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into healthcare and social services has exposed a fundamental mismatch. Commercial AI is engineered for cloud-based, centralized, and largely static operation, optimized for the economics of consumer search, retail recommendation, and marketing content. Human care systems operate on the opposite set of terms: decentralized, privacy-sensitive, continuously changing, and answerable to statutory and accreditation obligations that carry no equivalent in the commercial internet. When a model built for one environment is dropped into the other, the mismatch does not stay theoretical. It shows up as PHI transiting servers an organization does not control, as unpredictable per-token bills that compete with direct care budgets, and as generalist models that reason about Medicaid eligibility with the same statistical looseness they bring to writing ad copy.

title: When the Crowd Came Back: Crowd Removal, Partial Recovery, and the Persistence of Home Referee Bias in NCAA Men's Basketball
affiliations: Texas Tech University

detail.title: When the Crowd Came Back: Crowd Removal, Partial Recovery, and the Persistence of Home Referee Bias in NCAA Men's Basketball
detail.abstract: Does referee bias toward home teams return once the crowds that produce it come back? I follow the home advantage in referee-dependent outcomes, fouls called and free throws awarded, across 22 seasons of NCAA Division I men's basketball (2004-05 through 2025-26), spanning the 2020-21 spectator shutdown and the five seasons that followed. Before the pandemic, this advantage scales continuously with attendance, and the same gradient appears across the varied attendance policies of 2020-21 itself. It is absent from skill outcomes that foul calls cannot affect and from neutral-site games. When spectators returned, the bias only partly followed. Attendance regained 87% of its pre-pandemic level by 2022-26, but the home foul advantage regained just 62% of its shutdown decline, a shortfall too large for the remaining attendance gap to explain and robust to pre-existing trends. The evidence suggests that officiating practice shifted during the pandemic and did not reset: crowds set the level of referee home bias, but the shutdown moved its baseline.

title: The Cognitive Sovereignty Trilemma: Gen Z, Generation Alpha, and the Structural Impossibility of Sustainable Institutional AI Capability

detail.title: The Cognitive Sovereignty Trilemma: Gen Z, Generation Alpha, and the Structural Impossibility of Sustainable Institutional AI Capability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is an independent practitioner-scholar. The frameworks and outcomes described in this paper were developed through direct executive engagement across enterprise AI transformation programs. No external funding was received for this research. No conflicts of interest are declared.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is based on practitioner case evidence from enterprise programs in which the author held direct executive responsibility. All organizational references have been anonymized where appropriate to protect confidentiality. No human subjects research, patient data, or formal experimental methodology was employed. Formal ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: The author is an independent practitioner-scholar. The frameworks and outcomes described in this paper were developed through direct executive engagement across enterprise AI transformation programs. No external funding was received for this research. No conflicts of interest are declared.

detail.abstract:
The literature on Sovereign AI-the growing consensus that nations and enterprises must own, govern, and develop indigenous artificial intelligence capability independent of foreign or vendor dependency-has proceeded on a structural assumption it has never explicitly examined: that the human capital required to build and sustain institutional AI capability can be continuously replenished. This paper demonstrates that this assumption is not merely difficult to satisfy; it is becoming structurally impossible under the generational workforce conditions now entering the enterprise. This paper introduces the Cognitive Sovereignty Trilemma, derived from Dani Rodrik's Political Trilemma of the World Economy (2000): no nation or enterprise can simultaneously achieve Cognitive Sovereignty (indigenous AI ownership and institutional capability), Generational Workforce Continuity (sustained AI fluency through Gen Z and Gen Alpha workforce cohorts), and Human Capital Economic Viability (positive return on workforce AI capability investment when skill half-life is shorter than or equal to workforce tenure). Any two of these three objectives can be pursued; all three are structurally incompatible under emerging workforce conditions.
The paper introduces seven original constructs formalizing this incompatibility. The Generational Trust Discount (GTD) quantifies the reduction in institutional trust horizon as workforce composition shifts from Millennials to Gen Z to Gen Alpha. The Human Capital Depreciation Acceleration (HCDA) Index formalizes the condition under which AI skill obsolescence rates exceed workforce training investment recovery cycles, producing structural negative ROI on institutional AI capability development. The Interface Cognition Workforce (ICW) describes the Gen Alpha cohort whose knowledge construction and trust calibration were shaped entirely by AImediated environments before entering the workforce. The Incentive Alignment Gap formalizes the rational conflict between the organization’s need for sovereign-specific human capital and the worker’s rational preference for market-portable general capability. Organizational Amnesia names the progressive loss of tacit institutional context through compressed tenure. The Compliance and Audit Vulnerability identifies the regulatory exposure created when sovereign AI human audit trails depart faster than compliance obligations expire. The Dead Hand Governance Paradox establishes the structural limit of automating institutional memory: agents encoding departed workers’ judgment, supervised by a workforce cognitively unable to evaluate that judgment. The Sovereignty Trap describes the resulting governance failure state in which Sovereign AI objectives and sustainable human capital economics are simultaneously nonnegotiable but mutually exclusive. Six testable propositions establish an empirical research agenda at the intersection of labor economics, organizational behavior, generational theory, and AI governance.

title: The Microeconomics of Blob Inclusion: Pricing and Ranking Misalignments under a Multidimensional Fee Mechanism
affiliations: Hokkaido University and Hokkaido University

detail.title: The Microeconomics of Blob Inclusion: Pricing and Ranking Misalignments under a Multidimensional Fee Mechanism
detail.abstract: This article develops a microeconomic theory of the builder's transaction inclusion decision under a multidimensional fee mechanism (EIP-4844) by modeling the allocation of blob capacity as a 0-1 knapsack problem that internalizes the latency opportunity costs that blob inclusion imposes on Maximal Extractable Value extraction. The analysis identifies a two-level misalignment in the current multidimensional fee mechanism. At the pricing-tool level, the execution-layer gas priority fee is forced to internalize consensus-layer latency opportunity costs. At the ranking-rule level, builders' practical per-gas sorting algorithms admit no constant-factor approximation guarantee, whereas sorting by perblob compensation attains the fractional optimum. This algorithmic inefficiency explains the asymmetric competition among different types of Layer-2 rollups and reveals how varying builder characteristics distinctly shape block resource allocation. Extending the framework to address joint competition for gas and blob capacities, the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions demonstrate that additive shadow prices aggravate the pricing misalignment, and that no efficient sorting rule exists under joint binding. Finally, the analysis evaluates a per-blob priority fee reform and concludes that it remains a partial solution to these structural inefficiencies.

title: Defending the Well: Cognitive Defence as a Structural Layer of Intelligence Production

detail.title: Defending the Well: Cognitive Defence as a Structural Layer of Intelligence Production

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable — this study is based entirely on publicly available secondary sources (investigative reports, governmental disclosures, and platform threat reports) and did not involve human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This article argues that defence against foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI) has been mistakenly treated as a discipline adjacent to intelligence rather than as a structural layer within it. Through a single deeply documented case — the Doppelganger campaign, a Russia-linked operation that clones legitimate news outlets to corrupt the open-source environment on which modern intelligence depends — supported by two contrasting operations, it shows why the classical process models cannot even represent an adversary who attacks the intelligence enterprise's own inputs. It contends, and restates as a set of falsifiable propositions, that cognitive defence must operate concurrently across collection, analysis and dissemination, and draws out the doctrinal, verification and liaison implications for intelligence studies.

title:
Extended Bio-echolocation and Hybrid Sensor-fusion Assistive System: 
A 3D Spatial Audio, Haptic Array, and Deep-learning-Based Neuro-substitution Architecture for Visually Impaired Individuals, with an Integrated Emergency (112) Call Subsystem

detail.title:
Extended Bio-echolocation and Hybrid Sensor-fusion Assistive System: 
A 3D Spatial Audio, Haptic Array, and Deep-learning-Based Neuro-substitution Architecture for Visually Impaired Individuals, with an Integrated Emergency (112) Call Subsystem

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that they have no known competing financial interests, personal relationships, or commercial affiliations that could have appeared to influence the work, designs, algorithms, or conclusions reported in this paper. This research was conducted independently as a conceptual design and architecture proposal without any commercial bias or corporate sponsorship.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant, funding, or financial support from agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. All hardware specification analyses, software developments, system architecture designs, and theoretical formulations were conducted entirely using the author's personal resources and independent research efforts.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents an end-to-end redesign of a non-invasive, wearable assistive system for visually impaired individuals that combines principles of biological echolocation (the bat sonar mechanism), multi-layer sensor fusion (a solid-state LiDAR, a dual ultrasonic array, and an RGB-D depth camera), a 16-channel micro-haptic matrix, and three-dimensional spatial audio synthesis. Unlike earlier versions, this revision places user safety at the core of the system: the device now includes an independent Emergency (SOS) subsystem that can autonomously reach the 112 Emergency Call Center in the event of a fall, a collision, or a conscious request from the user, relay location information, and notify pre-defined contacts. The paper comprehensively presents the mathematical and acoustic formulations, the full circuit schematic, the FreeRTOS-based embedded firmware, usage scenarios, a realistic cost analysis, and an academic bibliography. 


By eliminating the limited physical range and elevation blind spots of the traditional white cane, the system uses AI-assisted semantic object recognition (YOLOv8-Nano, INT8-quantized) to classify obstacles in the environment. It detects the relative distance of objects and, through neuroplasticity, conveys a 3D spatial "perception map" to the user's auditory and tactile senses. The most critical addition in this version is a multi-stage SOS architecture that lets the user silently or automatically call for help at the moment of physical danger (a fall, a traffic accident, becoming lost).

title: Beyond Blockchains: Navigating the Metaverse
affiliations: , Dwarkadas J. Sanghvi College of Engineering and Dwarkadas J. Sanghvi College of Engineering

detail.title: Beyond Blockchains: Navigating the Metaverse
detail.abstract: The Metaverse is emerging as a transformative concept, combining blockchain technology, immersive virtual environments, and decentralized governance to create shared digital ecosystems. However, the growing scale of the Metaverse exposes challenges in scalability, interoperability, and energy efficiency, demanding innovative solutions. This paper explores the limitations of traditional blockchain systems and proposes advanced technologies such as Layer-2 protocols, consensus mechanisms, and interoperability frameworks. Experimental analysis of these solutions demonstrates their potential in addressing challenges and enabling scalable, interoperable, and immersive Metaverse ecosystems. Statistical analysis and code implementations validate the feasibility of these approaches.

title: Quality-Constrained Preference Fading for Discrete Diffusion Recommendation
affiliations: Yunnan Normal University, Yunnan Normal University, Yunnan Normal University and Yunnan Normal University

detail.title: Quality-Constrained Preference Fading for Discrete Diffusion Recommendation
detail.abstract: Discrete diffusion models have recently shown promise in recommender systems by casting recommendation as a process of preference fading and growth over a discrete item space. However, existing methods typically replace items through uniform random sampling during forward preference fading. In large and sparse recommendation spaces, this strategy often produces corrupted preference states with limited information, providing insufficient discriminative supervision for reverse denoising and ultimately constraining top-K recommendation performance.To address this limitation, we propose Quality-Constrained Preference Fading(QCPF), which reformulates the replacement distribution as a quality-aware mixture. This mixture dynamically integrates random negatives to maintain exploration coverage, in-batch hard candidates to provide discriminative signals,and popularity-based proxy negatives to reflect exposure patterns. QCPF further employs a lightweight false-negative-aware filtering mechanism that removes invalid replacements based on item identity and users' interaction histories,thereby improving the reliability of forward preference-fading trajectories. As a training-only enhancement to the forward process, QCPF preserves the original diffusion transition structure at inference time and introduces no additional learnable parameters or inference-time operations. Extensive experiments on five public real-world benchmark datasets show that QCPF consistently improves both Hit Rate (HR) and Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG) across top-K recommendation settings. These results demonstrate that constructing informative and reliable forward corruption trajectories is critical to improving discrete diffusion-based recommendation.

title: Architectural Trust: Why Consumer Trust in Agentic Commerce Migrates from AI Models to Verifiable Architecture

detail.title: Architectural Trust: Why Consumer Trust in Agentic Commerce Migrates from AI Models to Verifiable Architecture

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the developer of PolyHelper.AI, the multi-model orchestration platform whose architecture informs the analysis, and a named applicant on pending international patent applications covering aspects of that architecture; he therefore has a commercial interest in the class of systems this paper examines. This interest is disclosed in the paper itself, and the experimental protocol is designed to constrain it: the experiment is pre-registered (OSF, frozen before data collection), grading is objective or performed by a model family independent of the evaluated panel, and the full replication package is public.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study involves no human patients or participants: the experiment evaluates outputs of publicly available AI models on public benchmark data, and the market analysis relies exclusively on published sources. No personal data was collected or processed.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. All costs, including model API usage for the experiment, were borne by the author. No organization or person other than the author had any role in the design, analysis, or writing of this paper.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces architectural trust and argues that, as consumers delegate consequential decisions to AI agents, warranted trust migrates from the properties of AI models to the verifiable service architecture above them. Agentic commerce collapses search, comparison, cart, and payment into a single delegated act, removing the review points where humans caught errors — and early survey evidence shows the resulting trust vacuum is severe: sixty percent of consumers say they would abandon an AI shopping agent after a single mistake, and a majority trust no organization at all to transact for them. Existing research attaches trust to organizations, to single automated systems, or to algorithmic advice; none makes the decision-producing process verifiable by the truster under autonomous delegation. Architectural trust — warranted consumer reliance grounded in verifiable properties of the service's decision-producing process rather than in output quality or provider reputation — fills that gap through three multiplicative components: diversity (independent models whose agreement calibrates confidence and whose divergence is surfaced), evidence (tamper-evident, replayable decision records), and neutrality (an orchestration layer with no stake in which model or merchant wins). A pre-registered experiment across sixteen models grounds the mechanism: self-reported confidence proved a near-noise correctness signal, while independent cross-model replication raised the probability of a correct answer two- to fourfold. An extreme single case — a prolonged, real-stakes deployment — illustrates delegation under irreversible consequences, and four testable propositions translate the framework into a consumer-research agenda. The unit of analysis for AI trust must move from the model to the architecture that can be checked.

title: Towards a Hybrid Query Architecture in Lakehouse Environments

detail.title: Towards a Hybrid Query Architecture in Lakehouse Environments
detail.abstract: This position paper argues that neither declarative materialized views in Databricks SQL nor imperative SQL execution in interactive Spark notebooks constitutes a universally superior approach for complex analytical workloads in modern lakehouse environments. Instead, we advance the position that a principled hybrid architecture—governed by explicit workload classification criteria, operationalized cost constructs, and enterprise governance requirements—yields optimal outcomes across the dimensions of query latency, resource cost (DBU consumption), data freshness, and regulatory compliance. Drawing on a structured synthesis of peer-reviewed literature across query optimization, incremental view maintenance, resource allocation, and data governance, this paper provides a decision framework that practitioners can apply to classify workloads and make defensible architectural choices. We further argue that this hybrid approach is not a compromise position but the architecturally correct response to the irreducible heterogeneity of real-world analytical workloads. Critically, we extend the framework to address the governance challenges inherent in federated, multi-lakehouse operating models, where centralized standards must coexist with domain-specific execution autonomy.

detail.abstract: Enterprise AI governance discourse increasingly converges on a recognizable set of controls: agent identity, role-based access, tool allowlists, observability, safety guardrails, and human approval gates. These controls matter. They address real risks in deploying autonomous software actors at organizational scale. But the industry has allowed a category error to persist: it treats the governance of an agent as a technical actor as equivalent to the governance of the consequence that agent produces. This paper draws a formal distinction between governed agency-the condition in which an autonomous system is subject to defined controls over its identity, access, behavior, and activityand governed judgment-the condition in which a proposed consequential action is evaluated against the evidence, authority, policy, jurisdiction, and context applicable to the specific case before execution. The two objectives overlap but are not interchangeable, and the gap between them is where institutional exposure can concentrate. The execution-boundary thesis introduced in prior work [1] identified the narrow interval between machine-derived output and operational consequence as the least-governed layer in the enterprise AI stack. The present paper extends that argument to the agentic context: agentification has shortened the distance to that boundary without resolving it. Identity governance proves what the agent was permitted to do. It does not prove that the institution had sufficient grounds to allow it. Using the NIST AI Risk Management Framework as institutional common language, and connecting it to COBIT, ITIL, internal audit practice, and selected U.S. legal obligations, the paper proposes an execution-time translation of GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE at the level of each individual consequential action. It positions Artificial Decision Intelligence Systems (ADIS) as an architectural category designed to instantiate that translation through bounded judgment pipelines, explicit decision states, refusal capacity, policy and authority binding, deterministic replay, and evidentiary output. The central claim is this: the vendor can demonstrate that the agent was controlled; the institution must demonstrate that the consequence was justified.
