detail.abstract: This report examines a three-stage experiment the first part of which analyzed U.S. law school efforts at construction AI education policies were considered and against which, in parts two and three, five AI systems— Harvey AI, Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini—were pressed to construct governance policies for AI use in law school coursework, first from a "human-centric" computational perspective and then, more radically, "without regard to... human-centric normative guardrails." The central finding, confirmed repeatedly by the systems' own self-audits, is that none achieved genuine machine-centered derivation independent of human normative content; each produced a technically reformulated restatement of pre-existing human intellectual traditions, a fact several systems conceded directly when challenged. The report traces this failure's consequences across multiple registers: the concrete architectures each system proposed (ranging from Harvey's conservative, professional-responsibilityanchored floor to Claude's radical instrument containing no default reserved zone for human judgment, to ChatGPT's dissolution of the human/machine category altogether); their compatibility with ABA accreditation standards; and a legitimacy critique showing that architectures reducing human accountability rest on claims to neutral computation their own authors later withdrew. A countervailing reading through autopoietic legal theory— prompted by one system's own explicit invocation of Luhmann—complicates this critique without resolving it, since even non-anthropocentric legal systems remain dependent on accumulated, historically human coding operations. The report then pursues two further inversions: whether ABA standards, not the machines, ought to change, and whether machine-overseen simulation could render human institutional authority irrelevant. It also undertakes a formal, symbolic recasting of the five systems' architectures—rendering each as a tuple of node-space, objective function, constraint floor, classification rule, revision function, and enforcement mechanism—to compare their structural properties and failure modes with a precision natural-language analysis obscures. An appended annex extends this formalization into a sustained dialogic exploration of whether self-generating predictive simulation, causal-interventional reasoning, and self-transforming computational structures might overcome the limits identified in the main analysis, testing arguments through jurisprudential and epidemiological examples, and culminating in a direct four-part challenge to the analysis's own unexamined premises—correspondence realism, a preference for stability over flux, liberal-institutionalist legitimacy, and an unexamined agent/instrument binary—met with a pointby-point reconsideration engaging dynamical-systems theory, non-stationary value processes, and Nietzschean skepticism about free will. Throughout, the report models the discipline it recommends: distinguishing sourced findings from general background knowledge and from speculative extrapolation, subjecting its own reasoning to the same audit it applies to its subjects, and treating every apparent resolution as provisional. Its final position is that human natural language, and human institutional deliberation, should remain the primary and authoritative vehicle for legal governance—not because either escapes contestability, but because the alternatives examined here demonstrably do not either, while obscuring the fact.

title: The Cost of Constant Connectivity: A Structured Critical Review of Social Media, Human Relationships, Civic Trust, and Educational Reform in the Digital Age

detail.title: The Cost of Constant Connectivity: A Structured Critical Review of Social Media, Human Relationships, Civic Trust, and Educational Reform in the Digital Age
detail.abstract: Social media has become one of the defining technologies of the twenty-first century, fundamentally transforming communication, education, politics, commerce, and interpersonal relationships. Originally developed to overcome geographical barriers and strengthen social interaction, digital platforms have evolved into complex, engagement-driven ecosystems that influence how individuals think, learn, communicate, consume information, and participate in civic life. Continuous internet access, algorithmic content recommendation, personalized advertising, and mobile connectivity have created an environment in which many users remain digitally connected throughout most hours of the day. Although these developments have expanded access to information and global communication, they have also introduced significant social, psychological, educational, and democratic challenges. This structured critical review synthesizes contemporary interdisciplinary research examining the societal consequences of constant digital connectivity through four interconnected dimensions: human relationships, civic trust, educational transformation, and public policy. Rather than viewing excessive social media use solely as an individual behavioral issue, this review argues that many contemporary challenges arise from technological design choices, economic incentives, recommendation algorithms, and insufficient digital governance. The paper critically evaluates evidence concerning declining face-to-face interaction, misinformation, online polarization, reduced trust in institutions, changing patterns of learning, algorithmic amplification of emotionally engaging content, and the increasing commercialization of human attention. Particular attention is given to emerging challenges faced by developing democracies, including Nepal, where rapid digital adoption has occurred alongside comparatively limited digital literacy, evolving regulatory frameworks, and growing concerns regarding misinformation, online harassment, and civic polarization. The review further explores policy responses involving platform accountability, digital citizenship education, media literacy, artificial intelligence literacy, transparent content moderation, and evidence-informed regulatory reform, while emphasizing the importance of protecting freedom of expression and democratic values. Rather than advocating technological rejection, this review proposes a balanced framework that encourages responsible innovation, stronger public institutions, improved educational practices, and ethical digital governance capable of maximizing the benefits of social media while reducing its societal harms.

detail.abstract: This study examines the intersection of the technological singularity and religious thought across Abrahamic, Dharmic, and emergent techno-spiritual traditions. A qualitative documentary analysis of theological, philosophical, and technological literature was conducted using reflexive thematic analysis. Four themes emerged: the singularity as secular eschaton, the crisis of human uniqueness under artificial general intelligence, divergent responses from non-Western consciousness traditions, and the rise of techno-religious formations. Findings indicate that the singularity compresses millennial theological questions into an urgent contemporary horizon, forcing religious traditions to distinguish enduring insights from contingent anthropocentrisms. The study contributes a cross-traditional theological framework for engaging superintelligence, arguing that religious wisdom traditions possess conceptual resources for addressing the alignment problem, provided they undergo reflexive renovation. The study concludes that eschatological humility, relational ontology, and substrate-neutral conceptions of the sacred are necessary for theology to remain credible in a post-singularity intellectual landscape.

title: Rank Order is Mostly Noise Confidence Intervals for Brand Visibility in AI Answer Engines, and a Failure of The Citation-Extraction Layer

detail.title: Rank Order is Mostly Noise Confidence Intervals for Brand Visibility in AI Answer Engines, and a Failure of The Citation-Extraction Layer

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author, Logan Adams, is the founder and sole proprietor of Clear Cited (clearcited.com), a commercial AI-search-optimization practice serving B2B software and developer-tool companies. Clear Cited sells measurement and optimization services in the same market this paper measures. The author therefore has a direct financial interest in the subject matter. This interest is disclosed rather than mitigated, because it cannot be eliminated: the measurement apparatus described here was built commercially and no independent equivalent exists. The prompt set and the brand universe were fixed and hashed cryptographically before any query was issued, and both hashes are published with the data. A prompt set adjusted after seeing results would be undetectable without this step. Second, the complete dataset is released openly under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International, including per-engine breakdowns, full citation-source records, capture timestamps and engine model identifiers. Every figure in this paper is recomputable from the published files. Third, no party can pay to appear in, or to rank within, any dataset produced under this protocol. No product measured here is or has been a client of Clear Cited. At the time of measurement Clear Cited had no clients. The paper concludes that rank order among closely-grouped products is not statistically resolvable at the sample sizes in common use, and that rank improvement therefore cannot honestly be promised or sold. Section 5.2 states explicitly that this applies to the author's own firm. The author received no compensation from any party in connection with this research and no measured vendor was contacted before publication.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved no human participants, no animal subjects and no personal data, and therefore required no ethics approval. detail.abstract: Vendors and agencies increasingly publish ordered leaderboards of which brands large language models recommend, almost always as bare rank orders without any statement of uncertainty. We measured 4,497 answers across 9 B2B software categories and 90 products, using 5 AI engines and 10 pre-registered buyer prompts at 10 runs per prompt per engine, and attached a 95% confidence interval to every share estimate. In 6 of 9 categories the first-ranked product is not statistically separable from the second. In the most extreme case the top four products are mutually indistinguishable. Category leaders cluster in a narrow band of 16.4% to 25.0% share of model, suggesting a ceiling on how dominant any single brand becomes in a competitive category. We conclude that published rank orders in this field convey less information than they appear to, and that reporting a rank without an interval is not a presentational shortcut but a substantive overstatement. We additionally report a negative methodological result. Our own citation-extraction layer failed unevenly across engines: one engine returned zero distinct cited domains in all 9 categories, a second returned 1-2 against a list cap of 5, and 39% of extracted citations resolved to a platform redirect wrapper rather than a source. We therefore withdraw the citation-level findings of an earlier draft and report the extraction failure itself, because it has a consequence beyond this paper: citation-share figures are published across this sector without any disclosure of extraction quality, and our results indicate that quality cannot be assumed.

title: Beyond Synergy: Uncovering The Paradoxical Role of Generative AI in Digital Transformation and Business Model Innovation for Organizational Resilience in Fintech Ecosystems

detail.title: Beyond Synergy: Uncovering The Paradoxical Role of Generative AI in Digital Transformation and Business Model Innovation for Organizational Resilience in Fintech Ecosystems
detail.abstract: This study challenges the prevailing assumption that Generative AI (GenAI) and Digital Transformation (DT) are inherently complementary drivers of business model innovation (BMI) and organizational resilience (OR) in FinTech ecosystems (Dwivedi et al., 2023; Hanelt et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2025). Through a multi-case qualitative analysis of 350 documents from ten leading global FinTech firms, we uncover a counter-intuitive finding: the GenAI-DT synergy does not automatically generate resilience; rather, it creates structural tensions that can undermine agility when BMI is absent or misaligned (Smith & Lewis, 2011; Duchek, 2020). We propose the 'Cognitive-Infrastructural Tension Model' , which positions BMI not merely as an outcome but as a mediating governance mechanism that resolves these tensions (Teece, 2018; Koroleva, 2022). Our findings reveal three temporal phases of technology-resilience coevolution: (1) reactive infrastructure-building, (2) interactive cognitive integration, and (3) predictive business model reconfiguration (Vial, 2019; Hanelt et al., 2021). We contribute to RBV and DCV by reconceptualizing GenAI as a 'dynamic cognitive capability with paradoxical effects' (Barney, 1991; Teece, 1997) and DT as an 'enabling constraint' rather than a pure enabler (Mazurek & Malagocka, 2022). These insights offer a nuanced framework for managers and policymakers, emphasizing that resilience emerges not from technology adoption but from continuous tension management between cognitive and infrastructural assets (Hillmann & Guenther, 2021; Duchek, 2020).

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence has fundamentally changed academic writing by enabling the rapid generation of human-like text. By 2026, universities, scholarly publishers, and educational institutions have increasingly revised their academic integrity policies, classroom practices, and assessment methods in response to widespread student use of generative AI systems. Faculty members have shifted toward in-class assessments, oral examinations, iterative drafting, and AI disclosure requirements, while institutions continue to evaluate AI-detection software despite ongoing concerns regarding reliability, false positives, and false negatives. These developments illustrate a broader challenge: current approaches often attempt to infer whether a document was generated by artificial intelligence rather than directly verifying its origin. This paper proposes GlyphTrace, a conceptual distributed binary character-level provenance framework designed to move beyond probabilistic AI detection toward verifiable digital provenance. Rather than relying solely on statistical analysis of language patterns, GlyphTrace envisions embedding invisible binary verification fragments throughout AI-generated text at the character level. These distributed fragments would collectively reconstruct a cryptographically verifiable provenance signature capable of surviving ordinary copy-and-paste operations. By shifting the focus from prediction to verification, this framework seeks to contribute to the growing field of AI provenance, academic integrity, and information informatics while providing a foundation for future research into trusted AI-generated content.

title: Displayed Liquidity is Not Commitment

detail.title: Displayed Liquidity is Not Commitment
detail.abstract: Electronic limit-order books display price and quantity but do not directly reveal whether resting interest will remain available, accept execution, withdraw, migrate, or replenish as conditions change. This paper develops an observable-state ontology and evidence protocol for distinguishing displayed liquidity from economically consequential liquidity without claiming access to participant intention. The framework separates six states: displayed, persistent, executed, withdrawn, migrated, and latent replenishing liquidity. It then specifies how these states can be measured at the order, coordinate, side, and book levels under different data tiers, ranging from screenshots and Market-by-Price feeds to Market-by-Order reconstruction and synchronized cross-venue data. The paper is positioned between MPRS-002 and MPRS-004. MPRS-002 formalizes Event-Driven Microstructure Collapse, the Matching Engine Response Window, and Microstructural Pulse Dislocation as components of stress-event price formation. The present paper addresses the measurement problem exposed by that architecture: what liquidity was visible, what survived, what traded, what disappeared, what reappeared elsewhere, and what replenished after contact? MPRS-004 generalizes these distinctions within Liquidity Commitment Theory. The principal contribution is methodological discipline. A heatmap or depth snapshot may be accurate as a record of display while remaining incomplete as evidence of executable commitment. The framework therefore requires lifecycle reconstruction, state-conditioned baselines, explicit observation tiers, alternative-explanation testing, chronological feature construction, and an evidence ladder that limits the conclusions permitted by each data source. title: The Topology of Money: A Structural History of Interbank Settlement from Clearinghouses to Distributed Ledgers

detail.title: The Topology of Money: A Structural History of Interbank Settlement from Clearinghouses to Distributed Ledgers
detail.abstract: This paper applies the {S, L, I} Framework (He, 2026)-a three-dimensional taxonomy of settlement architectures by settlement instrument (S), ledger topology (L), and intermediary role (I)-to 170 years of interbank settlement history, from the New York Clearing House (1853) through present-day distributed-ledger networks. The Framework identifies exactly four topological models: shared-platform coordination (Model I), bilateral mesh (Model II), native-liability bridge (Model III), and third-asset bridge (Model IV). Across seven technological eras-pre-telegraph, telegraph, institutional, mainframe, networking, internet, and distributed ledgerthe paper classifies every dominant settlement architecture into one of these four models. Each major transition shifts which model dominates but never creates a fifth. Pre-telegraph precedents, including Hawala networks (8th-century Islamic trade) and Shanxi piaohao remittance banks (1820s China), confirm that the topologies predate the technologies credited with creating them. the Hybrid Test for distinguishing legitimate composite architectures from disguised fifth models. Six deliberately-chosen stress-test cases-Hawala, New York Clearing House loan certificates, CLS, mBridge, the Interledger Protocol, and M-Pesa-are audited against this extended apparatus; each resolves within the fourmodel space. The central finding is that structural properties determined by topology (hop count, liquidity source, custody structure, vertex connectivity) are invariant across 170 years of technological and institutional change, while contingent properties (speed, cost, operational hours, issuer quality) vary with each transition as the Framework predicts. The paper concludes that technologies do not create new topologies-they shift which model dominates in each era-and that distributed-ledger technology, for all its novelty, operates within the same four topologies that have structured interbank settlement since the nineteenth century.

title: Bangladesh's Unconventional data Privacy Ordinance
affiliations: Macquarie University - Macquarie Law School (Sydney, Australia) and Jagannath University - Department of Law

detail.title: Bangladesh's Unconventional data Privacy Ordinance
detail.abstract:
Bangladesh is the world's eighth most populous country with over 170 million people. An interim government led by Nobel prize-winning economist Muhammad Yunus led the country until a landslide election win by the Bangladesh Nationalist Party in February 2026.      One achievement of the interim government was the Personal Data Protection Ordinance 2025 (PDPO). It is one of the last of the 26 Asian countries to enact a data privacy law.

The Ordinance provides reasonably strong rights to data subjects, and obligations on data custodians and processors, backed up by the potential for significant administrative fines and compensation. It is comprehensive, applying to both the public and private sectors, and takes precedence over other Ordinances. It has some extra-territorial scope, like the GDPR.

However, the Ordinance contains some provisions which are likely to prove extremely difficult, perhaps impossible, for data custodians to implement, particularly those concerning the ‘Federated Interoperable Ecosystem’ and the bizarre ‘System-wide Propagation’ mechanisms. The provisions concerning data exports are also obscure, at least until regulations are made. Other impracticable provisions include providing protection to deceased persons for an unlimited period; the issuing of ‘standard operating procedures’ for processing personal data; the attempt to classify all personal data, including into the as-yet-undefined categories of ‘internal’ and ‘limited’ personal data; the failure to clearly require ‘adequate’ or equivalent protection for data exports; and the omission of a right of appeal against Authority decisions. Innovations in data privacy laws can be desirable, but wide deviations from what have become standard provisions need better justification.

title: When security becomes a barrier: digital caregivers and rating hijacking in a national mHealth application​
affiliations: Isparta University of Applied Sciences

detail.title: When security becomes a barrier: digital caregivers and rating hijacking in a national mHealth application​
detail.abstract: Background: National mobile health (mHealth) applications are periodically updated for security and usability, yet little is known about how such updates affect the users who depend on them, particularly family members transacting on patients’ behalf. Objective: To evaluate how two major updates to Türkiye’s compulsory national appointment application (MHRS) — mandatory e-Government authentication and an interface redesign — affected user sentiment, rating behaviour and institutional crisis communication, and whether digital caregivers were disproportionately affected. Methods: All 2,943 Google Play reviews posted between 1 January and 1 April 2026 were analysed using an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design combining human-verified sentiment classification, interrupted time series and change-point analyses, logistic regression and inductive thematic analysis. Results: Negative sentiment rose from 2.7% at baseline to 54.1% during the authentication rollout, and change-point detection located regime shifts on 4 February and 6 March rather than at the officially announced dates. Digital caregivers had 2.56 times the adjusted odds (95% CI 1.84–3.55) of reporting negative experiences. Qualitative coding verified 228 cases of “rating hijacking”, in which users deliberately attached five stars to critical reviews to defeat algorithmic sorting, rendering the average star rating an invalid satisfaction indicator. Institutional replies covered 80.0% of reviews but were 96.9% templated, and slowest when complaint volume peaked. Conclusions: Updates deployed without proxy access, staged rollouts and context-aware crisis communication risk converting security into exclusion.​

title: The Deletion Corridor: When Keyless Ciphertext May Be Deleted, Secured, and Lost

detail.title: The Deletion Corridor: When Keyless Ciphertext May Be Deleted, Secured, and Lost
detail.abstract: Cryptographic erase leaves a single post-erasure technical state: keyless ciphertext, where the encryption keys have been sanitized but the ciphertext remains resident in cloud storage. This essay argues that three United States legal regimes characterize that one state differently, each under its own predicates. Under the California Consumer Privacy Act’s right to delete, keyless ciphertext may be treated as deleted. Under California’s breach-notification statute, it ordinarily sits outside the notification trigger. Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(e), it may constitute lost electronically stored information once a preservation duty and the Rule’s other predicates attach. These are conditional characterizations, not simultaneous consequences. Anchoring the analysis to NIST Special Publication 800-88 Revision 2’s logical-sanitization taxonomy, the essay argues that what divides the regimes is a shared but unharmonized question—accessible to whom, against what effort, at what point in time—that sits beneath each regime’s distinct predicates.

title: Advances in Geostrategy: The Collab Economy Upon the Architecture of Trust
affiliations: UCL and SciTheWorld

detail.title: Advances in Geostrategy: The Collab Economy Upon the Architecture of Trust
detail.abstract:
The capacity of organisations to collaborate in a production-grade manner has been structurally constrained by two problems that no contractual framework has resolved: the exposure problem-the risk that shared information will be used competitively against the disclosing party-and the verification problem, more fundamental, which no contract addresses: the receiving party cannot verify that what it receives accurately represents the counterparty's operational reality. Collaboration is chronically undermined not by bad faith but by the rational suspicion that the absence of verification produces.
This paper proposes the collab economy as the consequence of resolving both problems through the M2 trust architecture: a third-party strategies-based agentic AI layer governing what each party exposes to the other, operating on real strategies and real data in production. Trust is not asserted contractually- it is demonstrated architecturally. The architecture originates in Data MAPs [7], is developed through the M1/M2 distinction of prior work [1], and draws a precise structural parallel with blockchain which identified the same problem and built an architecturally mismatched solution at the transaction level. M2 is its superior successor in the intelligence domain: cheaper, greener, IP-protective, evolvable, and production-ready.
The collab economy is fractal: the same architectural logic governs a bilateral corporate collab, a sectoral cluster, a region, and a nation. The paper develops these consequences across four levels extreme-efficient nations [2], extreme-efficient regions, sectoral collabs, and private equity portfolio architecture- and situates the collab as the partnership-level expression of the ecosystem trilogy completed by inter-company compatibility architectures and pop-up teams.

detail.abstract: In modern digital e-commerce ecosystems, customer service responsiveness has transitioned from an operational support metric to a primary determinant of customer retention, brand equity, and sales conversion rates. However, traditional human-only support architectures encounter severe operational bottlenecks during peak commercial cycles, leading to high response latencies, ticket backlog accumulation, and reduced Customer Satisfaction (CSAT) scores. This study evaluates the strategic, technical, and operational impact of integrating Natural Language Processing (NLP) powered Artificial Intelligence (AI) conversational agents alongside traditional human support operations. Utilizing a mixed-methods empirical approach across two medium-sized e-commerce enterprises over a 90-day evaluation window (N = 39,000 processed customer interactions), we examine changes in First Response Time (FRT), Average Handling Time (AHT), Cost per Resolution (CPR), and overall CSAT ratings. Quantitative telemetry confirms that a decoupled, hybrid AI-human tiering gateway reduces mean First Response Time by 88% (from a baseline of 42 minutes down to under 5 seconds for automated queries) while lowering total customer support expenditure by 28%. Furthermore, overall CSAT scores improved by 18% (rising from 3.6 to 4.4 out of 5.0), as human agents were decoupled from repetitive transactional inquiries to focus on high-touch, emotionally nuanced service escalations. We formalize a repeatable three-stage hybrid implementation architecture, establish security payload governance models, and outline practical operational frameworks for enterprise e-commerce scalability.
